India's real luxury market isn't fashion or cars
It's privacy.
Gated communities, private hospitals, business
class, VIP darshan.
The wealthiest Indians are paying to avoid other
Indians. That's the ultimate status signal.

A 3 crore flat in a gated community isn't about
Italian marble, it's about a guard at the gate who
decides who gets in.
Business class isn't about legroom, it's about a
curtain between you and 200 strangers.
A R15,000 private hospital consultation isn't
about better healthcare, it's about not sitting in a
room with 60 people waiting for one doctor.

We live in one of the most densely populated,
most chaotic, most sensorially overwhelming
countries on the planet.
And when you grow up surrounded by noise and
crowds and people everywhere in trains, in
markets, in your own home with 12 relatives, the
ultimate dream isn't a bigger house or a faster
car.
It's silence, space, and the ability to exist
without being pushed, stared at, or judged by
other Indians.

We don't talk about this because it sounds
elitist, but every person reading this who has
money is already spending on it.
You just don't call it luxury, you call it quality of
life or safety or good locality or premium
experience.
Strip away the euphemisms and what you're
paying for is distance from the crowd.

The brands that win next won't sell louder,
flashier, more visible products. They'll sell
invisibility, exclusivity, and the promise that you'll
never have to share your experience with
someone who didn't pay the same price.
In a country of 1.4 billion people, the scarcest
resource isn't gold or land or time, it's personal
space. And the people who have money will pay
almost anything to protect it.

Imagine you're in a massive auditorium with 362
million Indians.
Every age. Every income level. Every social
class.
And one by one, each person gets to walk on
stage and show off ONE thing about their life.

The billionaire shows his Rolls Royce.
The college student shows her new iPhone.
The maid shows her daughter's wedding.
The startup founder shows his "unicorn"
announcement.
The retired uncle shows his Goa vacation.
Everyone watching. Everyone comparing.
Everyone feeling something.
This is Instagram.

Here's what makes Instagram different from
every social space in history:
In real life, you only compare yourself to people
in your circle.
Your classmates. Your colleagues. Your
neighbors. Your relatives. Maybe 50-100 people
total.
On Instagram, your comparison group just
became 1 million people.
The delivery guy compares himself to Ranveer
Allahbadia.
The teacher compares herself to Komal Pandey.
The CA compares himself to startup founders.

The 725,000/month guy watches:
Millionaire's Maldives trip
• Friend's new car
Colleague's promotion
• Influencer's brand deal
His brain does this:
"Everyone's winning except me."
"I'm 28 and still here."
"What am I doing wrong?"
"Maybe I should take that loan for the car."

The Most Brutal Part:
In real life:
Poor people knew they were poor.
Rich people knew they were rich.
Middle class knew they were middle class.
Everyone stayed in their lane because they
couldn't see other lanes.
On Instagram:
Everyone sees everyone.
The lanes disappeared.

Result:
Middle class feels poor (comparing to rich)
Rich feel inadequate (comparing to richer)
Poor feel invisible (nobody's watching their
stage performance)
For the first time in history, every social class is
forced to watch every other social class perform
their best life.
And it's making everyone miserable.
This is the psychological experiment nobody
consented to.

But here's where it gets darker.
That 725,000/month guy watching everyone
else's highlight reel?
He doesn't just feel poor.
He feels like he's falling behind.
And when you feel like you're falling behind, you
don't save money.
You spend it. To catch up.

Result:
in 2024.
India's personal loan market hit 710 lakh crores
Credit card debt is at an all-time high.
Buy Now Pay Later is exploding.
People aren't spending more because they're
earning more.
They're spending more because they're
comparing more.

It's not aspiration.
It's desperation.
The psychological cost of being "left out" now
exceeds the financial cost of the EMI.
Instagram made invisibility more expensive than
debt.

Dhurandhar 2 is almost 4 hours long.
And people are sitting through every single
minute of it.
That tells you something important about how
cinema is quietly changing in India

Let's be honest. Four hours is a lot to ask of
someone.
You're buying a ticket, finding parking, dealing
with a crowded multiplex, and then sitting in a
dark room for the length of two average
Bollywood films back to back.
By every conventional rule of theatrical
distribution, Dhurandhar 2 should not be
working.But it is.

Part of it is simply that the film is really good.
Aditya Dhar shot 7 hours of footage across India
and Thailand. Rather than cut it to 2-2.5 hours
like every other director would have, he split it
into two films. Part 1 and Part 2 and each is
nearly four hours long.
He trusted that if the story was strong enough,
the clock wouldn't matter.
He was right.

But here's the insight nobody is talking about.
Dhurandhar 1 wasn't structured like a movie. It
was structured like a TV series broken into
chapters. Each chapter lands like an episode.
There's a cliffhanger, a revelation, a shift in tone,
and then the next chapter begins before you've
processed the last one.
People aren't sitting in the theatre for 4 hours.
They're binge-watching in the dark.
It felt less like watching a film and more like
finishing 6 episodes of something you couldn't
stop.

This is what Netflix and Prime have actually
done to Indian audiences.
They didn't kill the theatrical experience. They
rewired how people consume narrative.
An entire generation now has the stamina for
long-form storytelling. 8-episode seasons. 10-
episode series. 60 minutes per episode, no
interval.
Dhurandhar figured out how to bring that muscle
into the cinema hall.

Every filmmaker complains that OTT has ruined
the audience's attention span.
Aditya Dhar looked at the same audience and
said actually, they can sit for four hours if you
earn every minute of it.
The runtime isn't the problem. The pacing is.

The real insight here isn't about Dhurandhar.
It's about what Indian audiences are ready for.
They'll pay for a ticket, sit through four hours,
skip the interval samosas, and not check their
phone if you give them something that feels like
it's going somewhere.
Chapter by chapter. Episode by episode.

There's something bizarre about Indian
consumer behaviour.
• • •
I know a guy who spent 71,00,000 on a phone
and then spent 45 minutes last month looking
for a cracked APK because he didn't want to pay
799 for an app.
Another friend of mine bought a 73 lakh Royal
Enfield but refuses to pay 7500 a month for
Spotify, so he just sits through the ads like it's
nothing.
And every uncle who has spent 715 lakhs on his
daughter's wedding has also stood in a sabzi
mandi for 30 minutes fighting with a vendor over
750.

Same people, same wallets, and completely
opposite behaviour depending on what they're
buying.
We don't buy products. We buy proof.
That iPhone isn't really a phone, it's proof that
you've made it. That Enfield isn't transport, it's
proof that you're not like everyone else on the
road. That wedding isn't a ceremony, it's proof
that your family has standing in the community.
But Spotify Premium? Nobody knows you have
it. That 799 app sits invisibly on your phone
where no one will ever see it. And nobody at the
mandi is judging how much you paid for your
vegetables.

So the actual rule is this. Indians will happily pay
a premium for consumption that other people
can see, and will fight to the death to avoid
paying for consumption that nobody can see.
And once you notice it, you start seeing it
everywhere.
Zara is packed every single weekend because a
‹ 3,000 shirt is something people will notice, but
barely anyone in this country pays 7500 a year
for a news subscription because nobody knows
you have one.
Starbucks has a line out the door because a
7400 coffee can go on Instagram, while
meditation apps convert at 0.2% because your
mental health, at 71,500 a year, is invisible to
everyone but you.

My favourite example of all. people will buy an
780,000 sofa for the living room because guests
will sit on it, and then sleep on a 10-year-old
mattress in the bedroom because nobody ever
goes in there.

There's a second layer to this that took me even
longer to understand.
We are terrified of being taken advantage of, and
it's not really about the money at all. It's the fear
of looking like a fool, of paying for something
that everyone else somehow got for free.
This is why nobody ever admits they paid for
Tinder Gold, why every person you know "got a
discount" on everything they've ever bought,
and why perfectly sane people will spend two
hours hunting for a coupon code that saves
them F100.
The shame of overpaying is bigger than the joy
of owning, every single time.

And the flip side of that fear is that we're
genuinely, openly proud of getting things free or
cheap.
"Arre, let me just find it on Amazon during the
sale." "Why pay for it when you can download it
or borrow it or share someone's password?"
This isn't frugality, and I don't think it ever was.
This is sport.
Getting a discount is a social achievement that
you tell your friends about at dinner. Paying full
price is a social failure that you either hide or lie
about.

So if you're building anything in India, you can
skip the surveys and the focus groups, because
there's really only one question that matters.
Would your customer be embarrassed or proud
to tell their friends they bought your product?
If the answer is embarrassed, you're selling
invisible value, and that's the hardest thing to
sell in this country. If the answer is proud, you're
selling visible status, and half your marketing is
already done for you.

People don't move to Bangalore, Hyderabad,
Pune etc, just for the job.
• •
They move to become someone their hometown
wouldn't recognize.

The job is the excuse. The anonymity is the
reason.
• C
In your hometown, every purchase is witnessed.
Every relationship is reported back. Every life
choice gets an opinion from someone your
parents know. The surveillance isn't malicious.
It's just constant.
And after 22 years of it, a city where nobody
knows your family name feels less like a
relocation and more like oxygen.

This is why Bangalore, Pune, Hyderabad grew
the way they did and why Delhi and Chennai
didn't produce the same cultural shift.
Delhi pulls people who want proximity to power.
Chennai pulls people who want proximity to
family. Mumbai pulls people who want proximity
to fame.
But Bangalore pulled people who specifically
wanted distance. From something. The city
became a collection of deliberate escapees, and
that changes everything about how people live,
spend, and decide.

The most radical thing about Bangalore isn't the
startups or the pubs or the weather.
All they ask is your learn a little of their language
and respect their culture.
In return you get one of the only cities in India
where you're allowed to just be whoever you
showed up as. No one judges you here.
No context required. No explanation owed.
No committee deciding if you belong.
In a country that has opinions about everything,
that is not a small thing.
That is everything.

The Millennial Silence Problem
Why one of the most experienced generation on
the internet stopped talking and what it's
costing all of us.
Swipe to read -
→

Millennials are online more than ever. Scrolling at
2am, saving posts they'll never revisit,
consuming reels endlessly.
But they've stopped posting. Stopped writing,
stopped making videos, stopped sharing what
they know from years of actually doing the work.
An entire generation's worth of lived experience,
pattern recognition, and hard-won nuance is
sitting in people's heads doing nothing for
anyone.

In that silence, Gen Z took over the internet. Not
just the trends and aesthetics, the opinions. The
frameworks. The "here's how the world works"
content. Career advice, financial advice,
relationship advice, industry explainers.
They picked up the mic enthusiastically,
confidently, and often without the context that
only comes from having lived through enough
cycles to know what you don't know.

A 22-year-old with 8 months of work experience
makes a confident video titled "Why your
manager is gaslighting you" gets 4 million views.
Meanwhile a 37-year-old who's managed teams
for a decade, navigated three downturns, hired
and fired and been fired, has genuine scar tissue
from real leadership mistakes, watches the
video, thinks "this is so untrue," and says
nothing. Posts nothing and does nothing.
Everyone loses. The creator never gets a
thoughtful counterpoint. What's worse is the
audience builds mental models from a sample
size of one.

There's a term for what's happening and it's
called premature authority. Speaking with the
certainty of an expert from the experience base
of a beginner.
Financial advice from people who've never lived
through a real crash with actual money at stake.
Career advice from people who've had two jobs.
Parenting content from people who don't have
children, repackaging attachment theory PDFs
as lived wisdom.
The production quality is high. The confidence is
high. What's missing is the depth that only
comes from having been wrong enough times.

Algorithms don't measure depth of experience.
They measure engagement.
A confident, slightly provocative take from
someone with zero context will outperform a
nuanced "well, it depends" take from someone
who's actually seen both sides every single time.
And millennials know this.
Which is partly why they don't post. They think
"my take is too complicated for a reel." So they
say nothing. And the reductive version wins by
default.

This isn't theoretical. People are making career
decisions based on Linkedin posts written by
people who've had one job.
Financial decisions based on threads from
people who started investing in a bull market
and think that's just how it works.
Worldviews about politics, health, business,
relationships all shaped disproportionately by
people who haven't had the reps yet.
And the people who HAVE had the reps are right
there in the audience, rolling their eyes, saying
nothing.

Let me be clear this is a millennial abdication
problem. Somewhere around 2018-2019,
millennials collectively decided that posting was
cringe.
That it was for "influencers." They retreated into
group chats and dinner table rants that go
nowhere. They became the generation of "l
could write a whole post about this" but never
does.
By stepping back, they didn't opt out of the
attention economy. They handed the
microphone to whoever was willing to pick it up.

Your silence isn't noble. You have lessons,
frameworks, stories of failure and recovery that
could change how someone navigates a hard
decision.
Every day you don't share it, someone else fills
that gap with something shinier but thinner.
You don't need to become an influencer. You
don't need to post daily. Just occasionally write
down something you know to be true from
experience that you don't see anyone else
saying.
The internet doesn't need more content. It
needs more lived content

There's a generation in India earning 30 LPA that
genuinely feels poor.
And I know how that sounds. 30 lakhs is top 1%
of this country. Our parents would've called
relatives.
But this person opens a home buying app, sees
a 3BHK in Indiranagar for 2.8 crores, does the
EMI math in their head, and closes the app.

See, our parents had a ladder. Job, flat, car, kids,
retirement. Boring, but every step existed. You
could stand on it.
That ladder is broken now. In 2005 a flat cost
around 4-5 years of a decent salary. Today it's
12-15 years. Salaries went up 3x, property went
up 10x.

The flat was never just a flat. It was proof to your
parents, to yourself that you'd made it. And
when the flat becomes impossible, that need for
proof doesn't disappear. It just looks for a
smaller vehicle.
Psychologists actually have a name for this
compensatory consumption. When the real goal
gets blocked, people buy symbols of it instead.
And the substitute has to signal the same thing.
They buy the iPhone Pro Max. The boutique
gym. The expensive Ramen dinner that
obviously goes on Instagram.

Which explains so much of what you see around
you.
Your friend who "can't save" but has AirPods
Max. The 2k coffee subscriptions everywhere in
Indiranagar. Everyone has an aunty about it "this
generation doesn't know how to save, lifestyle
inflation"
", all that.
But it's not indiscipline. The money that
would've been a down payment is still doing
exactly what a down payment does - buying the
feeling of having arrived.

And I don't think this generation is being
irrational. Honestly the opposite.
They looked at a game that became unwinnable,
and instead of grinding for 15 years towards a
step that doesn't exist, they moved the game
somewhere it could actually be played.
The aspiration didn't die. It just changed
address.
So yeah, judge the iPhone if you want. But you
might be looking at the most rational financial
behaviour in the country right now.

Because of Instagram Psychologists, now

Your friend being 5 minutes late is disrespecting

India went from "therapy is for crazy people" to
"therapy is cool" in about four years.
Somewhere in that jump, an entire generation
learned the language of mental health without
doing the work of mental health.
• • •

The vocabulary arrived first. Trauma. Triggers.
Toxic people. Emotional unavailability.
Boundaries. Healing. Attachment Styles.
These words entered group chats, Instagram
captions, and dinner table conversations faster
than any awareness campaign could have
planned.
And for a while, it felt like progress.

But there's a difference between knowing the
words and doing the thing the words describe.
Knowing that avoidance is a trauma response
doesn't mean you stop avoiding. Knowing that
you have attachment issues doesn't mean
you've worked through them.
Knowing the name of the wound is not the same
as cleaning it.

Therapy in India became an aesthetic before it
became a practice.
The person who posts about "healing" has had
just two therapy sessions and stopped when it
got uncomfortable.
Everyone spoke about therapy but most of them
didn't actually go for therapy

Real therapy is uncomfortable in a way that
doesn't make good content.
• • •
You sit with someone for an hour and they ask
you questions you don't want to answer. You
leave feeling worse, not better.
You go home and think about something your
mother said in 1997 and feel an emotion you
don't have an Instagram caption for. You cancel
next week's session because it's too much. You
come back anyway..

The cruelest part is what this does to the people
around them.
A person armed with therapy vocabulary but not
therapy depth is genuinely more difficult to be in
a relationship with than someone who never
encountered any of it. They can name your
behavior patterns before you can.
They can exit conversations by calling them
triggering. They can frame their own avoidance
as self-protection and yours as toxicity.
The vocabulary, without the work, becomes a
weapon with a wellness label on it.

Real therapy costs something. Time, money, and
more than anything else, the specific discomfort
of looking at yourself clearly for an extended
period without looking away.
Most people got as far as learning the language
and decided that was enough.
A generation that can diagnose everyone around
them but can't sit with their own discomfort for
more than ten minutes.
That's not a mental health revolution.

Every creative person you admire, the writer, the
filmmaker, the artist. They all have one thing
common.
They feel things more than most people. They're
highly sensitive people. But it's this sensitivity
that helps them create stuff no one else can

You know how some people can watch a sad
movie and walk out fine?
Creative people are still thinking about it three
days later.
A song comes on and they have to sit with it. A
conversation ends and they're replaying it at
midnight. A stranger's expression on the street
stays with them for weeks.
This is sensitivity. And it looks like a problem
until you realise it's actually a superpower
• • •

Here's the thing about making art.
You cannot move people with something that
didn't move you first.
You cannot write about grief you've never sat
inside. You cannot make someone feel seen if
you don't notice them in the first place.
Sensitivity is what gives creative people the raw
material. Everything else is just craft.

Sensitive people notice what the rest of us miss.
The shift in someone's tone when they're
pretending to be okay. The mood of a room
before anyone's said a word. The small,
throwaway moment that actually contains
everything.
Most of us filter this out. Creative people filter
none of it. They're walking around absorbing the
world at full volume, all the time.
That's exhausting. It's also where all the good
work comes from.

This is why creative people are hard to give
feedback to.
You think you're critiquing the work. They
experience it as a critique of themselves.
Because for them, it's the same thing. They
didn't just make something. They put a piece of
their interior life on the table in front of you. And
now you're telling them what's wrong with it.
That's not ego. That's just what real creative
work costs.

It also makes ordinary life harder than it looks.
A small conflict doesn't leave quickly. A negative
comment lands heavier than intended. They feel
the weight of things that other people shake off
in an hour.
They're not being dramatic. They're just built
differently. The same setting that makes them
feel deeply also means they can't switch it off
when they want to

We spend a lot of time telling sensitive people to
toughen up.
Grow thicker skin. Don't take things so
personally. Learn to detach.
And sensitive people spend a lot of energy
trying to do exactly that. Trying to feel less.
Trying to care less. Trying to be more like
everyone else.
It never works. And it costs them the very thing
that makes them good at what they do.

India has thousands of businesses doing 75-50
crore in annual revenue, with hefty margins and
you have never heard of a single one of them.
Not because they're hiding. Because they never
needed you to know about them.

There's a tiles manufacturer in Morbi, Gujarat
who has been supplying to builders across three
states for twenty two years.
No Instagram page, no founder Linkedin, no
Series A announcement on YourStory. No PR
firm on retainer. Just a factory, a distributor
network built relationship by relationship over
two decades, and a waiting list of buyers.
There's a packaged spice brand in Rajkot that
sells only through kirana stores in four districts
and does more revenue per SKU than D2C
brands with national ambitions and a Z40 lakh
monthly Meta ad budget.
There's a school uniform supplier in Tirupur who
locked in contracts with 200 schools and hasn't
had to acquire a new customer in eleven years.

None of these people are in your feed. None of
them went on Shark Tank. None of them have
raised a rupee from anyone.
Here's the thing nobody wants to say out loud.
The Indian startup ecosystem spent the last
decade deciding that the only businesses worth
celebrating are the ones that raised money, got
a TechCrunch mention, and showed up in
Inc42's funding roundup.
Somewhere along the way we confused
fundability with viability. We confused visibility
with success.
We built an entire culture that worships the loss-
making unicorn and walks straight past the
profitable business down the road that employs
forty people and has zero debt,

So what does this actually mean?
The playbook already exists. It's just not where
anyone is looking. It's not in a YC batch or a
Sequoia portfolio or a Shark Tank episode.
These businesses figured out the one thing the
entire startup ecosystem is still trying to hack its
way to. Customers who come back.
Margins that don't depend on a discount.
Growth that doesn't require a new funding round
to sustain itself.
You don't need a new framework. You need to
go study the people who never needed one.

India has 23 IITs. Thousands of engineering
colleges. Thousands of med schools.
One FTII in Pune. A handful of NID campuses. A
few design schools scattered across cities that
took decades to earn any credibility.
Performing arts? Journalism? Creative writing at
the level it deserves? You're looking at single
digits. Nationally.

India is the second largest film industry in the
world. One of the largest music markets. One of
the fastest growing design and advertising
economies.
We are producing creative output at industrial
scale with zero industrial infrastructure to train
the people doing it.
Most creative professional in India is essentially
self-taught.

And then we wonder why our films feel recycled.
Why our advertising looks imported. Why our
design sensibility hasn't found its own language
yet.
The answer is not talent. India has never had a
talent problem. Walk into any class 9 in any
small town and you'll find a kid who draws,
writes, composes, imagines things beautifully.

Engineering. Medicine. Law. CA. Commerce.
These are not just career paths. They are the
only paths the country decided to build roads to.
Everything else you figure out. You YouTube. You
beg for an internship. You explain to your family
why you are 24 and still "finding yourself."

The absence of institutions doesn't mean
creativity disappears. It means creativity
becomes a privilege.
If there are no schools, only people with
connections, money, or proximity to the industry
can enter it. The self-taught path is brutal.
Only those who can absorb years of financial
uncertainty without a credential survive it. Which
means Indian creative fields are
disproportionately populated by people who
could afford to figure it out.

We are not losing creative people to bad
choices. We are losing them to an absence of
infrastructure so complete that most of them
don't even know there was another door.
The question worth sitting with is-how many
great designers, filmmakers, writers, journalists,
found no roads, and became engineers instead?

Reels are dying in 2026. And the creators who
figured this out six months ago are already
winning.
Here's what nobody in the content game wants
to admit right now.

Let's look at what actually happened.
Instagram pushed Reels hard from 2020 to
2024, threw money at creators, gave them
insane reach, made everyone believe that if
you're not doing Reels you're invisible.
So every brand, every creator, every marketing
agency pivoted. Entire teams were hired just to
make 15-second videos. And for a while, it
worked.
Reach was up, views were up, everyone felt like
a genius.

But here's what the numbers are saying now.
Reel reach has dropped 35-40% compared to
early 2024.
The average Reel gets seen for 1.2 seconds
before someone swipes past it.
Completion rates are below 15% for most
creators. And here's the killer. Saves and shares
on Reels have collapsed because nobody
bookmarks a dancing transition or a trending
audio anymore.
The format got commoditized. When everyone is
making the same Reel with the same hook and
the same audio, nobody remembers any of
them.

Meanwhile, carousels quietly became the most
powerful format on Instagram and nobody was
paying attention.
Carousel posts are getting 2-3x more saves than
Reels. They're getting shared to DMs more than
any other format.
The average time spent on a carousel is 45
seconds to 2 minutes versus that 1.2 second
Reel swipe.
And here's what matters most is
carousels are driving actual conversions, actual
profile visits, actual follows. Not vanity views
that mean nothing.

Let me tell you why this happened. Reels were
designed for discovery.
You'd get shown to a million people who don't
follow you, they'd watch three seconds, maybe
like it, and disappear.
You were essentially renting attention from
strangers. Carousels do the opposite. They
reward depth. Someone who swipes through all
ten slides of your carousel actually cares about
what you're saying.
They're reading. They're processing. They're
saving it for later. That's not rented attention,
that's earned trust.

Here's the other thing nobody talks about.
Reels attract the wrong audience. I've seen this
with brands I've worked with and creators I
mentor.
A Reel goes viral, you get 10,000 new followers,
your engagement rate drops to 1.2%, and your
next five posts tank because Instagram just
brought in 10,000 people who followed you for
entertainment, not for what you actually do.
Carousels attract people who read. People who
think. People who save posts and come back to
them. That's your actual audience. That's where
the money is.

Think about it from the algorithm's perspective
too. Instagram's algorithm in 2026 is rewarding
time-on-post and saves more than its rewarding
views.
A Reel that gets 100K views but 12 saves is
algorithmically less valuable than a carousel that
gets 8K impressions but 400 saves and 200
shares. Instagram wants people to stay on the
app.
Carousels make people stay. Reels make people
scroll faster.

The shift is clear. Depth is beating
entertainment. Text is beating audio.
Teaching is beating performing. Carousels are
beating Reels.
The creators who understood this early are
building audiences that actually buy, that
actually trust them, that actually show up.
Everyone else is still chasing views and
wondering why their business isn't growing.
Stop chasing reach. Start building depth. That's
the game in 2026.

Imagine you're in a massive auditorium with 36
crore Indians. Every age, every income level,
every social class.
And one by one each person gets to walk on
stage and show off one thing about their life.

The billionaire shows his Rolls Royce. The
college student shows her new iPhone. The
maid shows her daughter's wedding.
The startup founder shows his unicorn
announcement. And the retired uncle obviously
shows his Goa vacation :)
Everyone watching everyone. And everyone
feeling something while watching.
This is basically Instagram.

Now here's the thing I find fascinating. For all of
human history you only compared yourself to
people in your circle. Your classmates, your
colleagues, your neighbours, your relatives.
Maybe 50-100 people max.
But on Instagram your comparison group
suddenly became a million people.
So now the delivery guy is comparing himself to
Ranveer Allahbadia and the school teacher is
comparing herself to Komal Pandey. Think about
how insane that is.

So a guy earning 25k a month opens the app
and watches someone's Maldives trip, his
friend's new car, his colleague's promotion,
some influencer's brand deal.
And his brain is quietly going - everyone's
winning except me. I'm 28 and still here. What
am I doing wrong. Maybe I should just take that
loan for the car.

And this is the part that took me the longest to
understand. Earlier, poor people knew they were
poor and rich people knew they were rich and
the middle class knew exactly where they stood.
Everyone stayed in their lane because you
literally couldn't see the other lanes.
Instagram removed the lanes

So now the middle class feels poor because
they're comparing to the rich. The rich feel
inadequate because they're comparing to the
richer.
And the poor feel invisible because nobody's
even watching their stage performance.
For the first time ever, every social class is
forced to watch every other social class perform
their best life.
It's basically a psychological experiment on a
billion people and nobody consented to it.

And when you constantly feel like you're falling
behind, you don't save money. You spend it. To
catch up.

Which explains so much of what's happening
around us. Personal loans in India crossed 10
lakh crores. Credit card debt at an all time high.
BNPL everywhere.
People aren't spending more because they're
earning more. They're spending more because
they're comparing more.

I spoke to a couple of psychologists about this
and one of them told me something that stayed
with me - the psychological cost of feeling left
out has now become bigger than the financial
cost of the EMI.
So the next time you feel that itch to buy
something after a scrolling session, just pause
and ask yourself if you actually want the thing.
Or if you just watched someone else walk on
stage with it.

"marriage material." Only 14% actually earn that.

arrogance. They're quietly stepping back
because the math doesn't work, the
expectations feel impossible, and the emotional
cost of trying to meet everyone's standards is
exhausting.

women aged 25-44 will be single. The highest
number in recorded history.

The Great Indian Middle Class Conundrum.
Everyone's spending more. Nobody's feeling
richer.
Swipe to read —

Our parents had a simple definition of "doing
well." Paid-off house. Government job or stable
private sector salary.
Fixed deposit at SBI. Maruti 800 in the parking
lot that they drove for 11 years without thinking
about upgrading.
They didn't need anyone to know they were
comfortable. They just were. And that was
enough.

Somewhere between Jio making the internet
free and Flipkart making No Cost EMI feel like a
human right, the entire definition of "respectable
middle class life" changed.
It's no longer about stability. It's about signaling.
The middle class today isn't defined by what
people have in their bank accounts.
It's defined by what they can make other people
believe they have in their bank accounts.

The Bali trip isn't a holiday. It's a credit card bill
split across 6 months that buys 14 Instagram
stories and one profile-worthy sunset photo
that'll be relevant for the next 8 months.
The Zara shirt isn't clothing. It's what someone
wears to a Koramangala cafe
Nothing is just a purchase anymore. Everything
is a production.

And the strangest part is that this isn't coming
from greed or vanity. It's coming from fear.
The fear of being perceived as "not doing well."
Three people from college posted Europe trips
last month. A cousin just bought a bigger
apartment. A colleague's wife showed up with
that bag. Nobody sat down and decided to
compete.
But the scoreboard is Instagram and everyone's
checking it whether they admit it or not. The
pressure isn't coming from one person. It's
coming from everywhere all at once and it never
switches off.

So someone earning 710-12 lakhs a year is now
living a lifestyle that was designed for someone
earning 725 lakhs.
The math doesn't work. It was never supposed
to work. But EMIs exist and credit cards exist
and "buy now pay later" exists and suddenly the
gap between what someone earns and what
someone displays can be financed quietly
enough that nobody notices.

The worst part is that everyone knows. The
person spending knows the Bali trip is stretching
the credit card.
They know the car EMI is eating 40% of their
take-home. They know the F3,500 dinner was
for the story and not the food because honestly
nobody even remembers what they ordered.
But stopping feels impossible because stopping
means being the first person in their circle to
stop. And the first person who stops performing
looks like they failed. So everyone keeps going.
Everyone knows everyone else is also
pretending. Nobody says it out loud. Because
saying it out loud breaks the entire game and
nobody wants to be the one holding the mirror.

The great Indian middle class conundrum isn't
about money.
It's about the fact that an entire generation is
spending to perform a version of life they can't
actually afford, in front of an audience that's
doing the exact same thing, and nobody can
stop first because stopping looks like losing.
Our parents didn't have this problem. Not
because they were wiser. But because nobody
was watching. The real luxury today isn't the trip
or the car or the sneakers.
It's being financially comfortable enough to not
care whether anyone knows.

Enough. I don't want to hear another word about
Al.
I don't care if Claude beat GPT or Grok beat
Gemini or some new model called Higgs or Flux
or whatever Silicon Valley nonsense dropped
this week.
I don't want to know the benchmark. I don't want
to see the demo. I don't want another LinkedIn
bro telling me "this changes everything."
I just want to drink my chai, stare at something
that isn't a screen, and exist like a normal human
being for five consecutive minutes.

I spent two hours last week trying to buy
headphones, and I think it explains something
about us.
Every person I talk to these days is living inside
the grass is greener problem, and there's
actually a name for it.

So last week I wanted new headphones. Simple
task. I opened one tab, and literally two hours
later I had 20 tabs open.
I was reading about driver materials and whether
the company's factory in Vietnam treats workers
well. And why one reviewer said the bass was
muddy and another said it was perfect.
I closed my laptop having bought nothing and
feeling worse than when I started.

Barry Schwartz, the psychologist, has a word for
this. He calls it maximizing. A maximizer is
basically someone who cannot make a choice
until they are sure it is the best possible choice.
The problem is that best possible keeps moving
because there is always one more review, one
more reel, one more friend who bought
something slightly better

The other type he talks about is the satisficer.
And I really like this word because it sounds like
a compromise but it's actually not.
A satisficer first figures out what they genuinely
need, like I need headphones that don't hurt my
ears after an hour and cost under 25k, then
picks the first thing that meets that and stops
looking.
Which sounds easy but honestly I don't think
l've done it once this year.

And we are all becoming maximizers by default.
Every app shows you the alternative.
You're looking at a job and the app is already
showing you three more. You're on a date and
someone's phone buzzes with a match.
Even picking a cafe in Koramangala has become
a 20 minute Google Maps exercise. The
environment is basically built so that you never
feel done.

And the thing Schwartz found, which I keep
thinking about, is that maximizers often do end
up with slightly better outcomes, slightly better
salary, slightly better headphones, and still
report being less happy with them. Because in
their head the comparison never actually closed.
So maybe the question isn't how do I find the
best one. Maybe it's becoming a saticficer

MODERN DATING CAN'T BE FIXED

dating and the responses were wild.

matches but all garbage"
Men: "Women only want the top 10%. I get zero
matches"

actually serious"

FIRST ISSUE:
We're psychologically broken now
Once you've tasted unlimited choice, your brain
can't commit to one person anymore.
Every argument → "I have options"
Every annoying habit → "I could find better"
Every normal boring evening → "Did I settle?"
You don't even need the app on your phone.
Just knowing you COULD download it again
destroys your ability to work through basic
relationship friction.

SECOND ISSUE:
Instagram destroyed contentment
You're not just comparing your partner to other
people.
You're comparing your entire RELATIONSHIP to
everyone's best moments.
That friend's Goa proposal. Your colleague's
"perfect" anniversary post. Some influencer's
matching couple outfits at the airport.
Your completely normal, actually good
relationship feels average. Not because it is.
But because you're benchmarking against
fiction.

THIRD ISSUE:
We forgot how to put in effort
Apps made dating frictionless. No social risk. No
real rejection. Just swipe, unmatch, move on.
Now when actual relationships need work -
tough conversations, boring phases, conflict
resolution - people just... leave.
"Why fix this when I can start over with someone
new?"
Cool. That new person will also have problems.
And you'll leave again. Loop continues.
We've been trained to treat people like they're
replaceable.

FOURTH ISSUE:
Nobody wants to admit the real answer
The solution isn't an app update.
It's not "better algorithms."
It's accepting that serious relationships require:
• Intentional effort (not convenience)
• Uncomfortable vulnerability (not
curated perfection)
• Real-world interaction (not endless
optimization)
But that's hard. And boring. And doesn't scale.
So we keep pretending the next app feature will
fix what's fundamentally a human commitment
problem.

So here we are:
Apps rewired our brains to never be
satisfied
Social media made good
relationships feel inadequate
The economics are fundamentally
broken
We can't commit even when we find
something decent
No app redesign fixes this. No "go offline"
strategy fixes this. This is a people problem at
scale.
If you genuinely think there's a solution, tell me.
Because from where I'm sitting, this thing is
unfixable.

If you want something different, you need to do
something different.
Delete the apps for 90 days. Join communities
around your actual interests..
Talk to people IRL. Go on dates set up by friends
who know you.
Will it be slower? Yes.
More awkward? Absolutely.
Smaller dating pool? Definitely.
But you'll be selecting from people who can
handle friction, commit to plans, and exist
beyond a profile.
The apps didn't break dating.
We let them replace the work relationships
always required.

bizarre hierarchy.
At the top: Funded founders who speak well and
post consistently. Whether or not they've built
anything profitable is irrelevant. They have
"credibility" because they raised capital.
In the middle: Consultants, coaches, and
content creators who've studied these founders
and now teach their frameworks. Most have
never run a business. But they have Canva
templates and a R15,000 course.
At the bottom: People who've actually been
profitable for decades. No content. No audience.
No frameworks. Just cash flow.
We worship the top. We pay the middle. We
ignore the bottom.

Now let me tell you about the founder your feed
loves.
Raised 750Cr. Beautiful office in HSR Layout.
200-person team. Spoke at 4 conferences this
year. 47K Linkedin followers. Featured in
YourStory, Economic Times, and a podcast with
800K views.
Burning $1.2Cr a month. Revenue hasn't crossed
R18Cr in 3 years. Unit economics are negative.
Last round was a down round they called a
"strategic restructuring."
But he sounds smart in interviews. So we listen.

India's real business knowledge doesn't live on
the internet.
It lives in trader families in Surat who've figured
out global diamond distribution without an MBA.
In textile manufacturers in Tirupur who export to
40 countries and still do accounting in a
notebook.
In kirana store owners who manage 3,000 SKUS,
extend credit to 200 families, and maintain a
95% collection rate — all from memory.
In restaurant families in old Delhi running the
same kitchen for 4 generations with zero

The best business minds in India don't have
followers. They have margins.

sounding person turned out to have zero
medical training.

hierarchy. The person who's doing well but never
posts about it is the real one. The person who's
sharing wins, putting out content, building in
public is the tryhard. The cringe one. The one
who's probably not that successful because if
they were, they wouldn't need to announce it.
You've seen this play out. Someone you know
starts posting reels or writing on Linkedln and
the group chat lights up with "bro's really
becoming an influencer."
That one line does more damage than any
algorithm ever could.

So millennials learn to perform disinterest.
They'll have a genuine insight and keep it for a
dinner conversation instead of a post.
They'll start writing something, get halfway
through, and decide it sounds too "look at me."
They'll say "I'm just not a content person" like
it's a personality trait when really it's armour.
Because the moment you put yourself out there
with any real intent, you risk losing standing
among the only audience whose opinion actually
keeps you up at night. Not followers. Not
strangers. Your own friends.

And here's where it gets painful. The internet
doesn't care about your friend circle's hierarchy.
The internet doesn't reward quiet. It doesn't go
looking for the smartest person who chose not
to post. It rewards whoever showed up and said
here, this is what I think, and here's why it
matters.
So the 21 year-old with no experience but no
cringe reflex builds the audience. And the 30
year-old with twice the insight goes home and
complains about how the internet rewards
performance over substance.
I've watched this happen to people I know. I've
been this person.

And the worst part is that millennials already
know this. They follow creators younger than
them. They see people with half their experience
building audiences on insights they've had for
years but never posted.
They know the game. They understand
distribution. They've read the books and listened
to the podcasts. They have every tool and every
framework.
The only thing they don't have is the ability to hit
post without feeling like they're performing. And
that one missing thing is the whole thing.

So if you're a millennial who wants to sell
yourself, just know that the resistance you feel
isn't about the content. It's about identity. You're
not afraid of the algorithm.
You're afraid of what your college roommate will
think. What your ex-colleague will text someone.
What your parents will ask at dinner. And that
fear is real.
And getting over that fear is important if you
want to get more opportunities.

There's a specific kind of guilt that creative
people carry. And it has nothing to do with the
work.
It's the guilt of charging well for something that
came naturally to them.

You'll see it everywhere. The designer who
quotes R15,000 for a logo that took her 6 hours
but 6 years of taste to develop.
The writer who charges per word because
charging per idea feels arrogant.
The filmmaker who says "let's figure out the
budget later" because talking money feels like it
cheapens the art

Creative people didn't see their parents enjoy
work. Work was supposed to be hard. So when
something comes naturally to you writing,
designing, making, it doesn't feel like work.
And if it doesn't feel like work, it doesn't feel like
it deserves money. You're not charging for a
skill. You're charging for something that felt
easy. And easy feels like cheating.

A CA bills for hours. A lawyer bills for hours. The
input is visible. But a designer who cracks a logo
concept in the shower can't explain what she's
billing for. The thinking is invisible. The taste is
invisible.
The 10 years that made that shower moment
possible are invisible. So the creative person
discounts the outcome because even they can't
see the input clearly.

Creative people don't see themselves as
businesses. They see themselves as artists who
happen to need money. So every negotiation
feels like a betrayal of identity.
Charging well means admitting you're in the
market. And admitting you're in the market
means you're not purely about the craft
anymore.
The guilt is really about protecting a self-image
that was never sustainable.

So creative people do this bizarre thing. They
separate the making from the earning. They'll
obsess over a font for three days but won't
spend three minutes negotiating a rate.
They'll perfect a pitch deck for someone else's
startup but won't invoice for it on time. The craft
gets devotion but the commerce gets apology.

And here's where it gets worse. The market
reads your guilt as a signal. When you
undercharge, clients don't think you're
generous.
They think you're not good enough to charge
more. Your discount doesn't buy loyalty. It buys
disrespect.
The same client who paid you 720,000 will pay
an agency 72,00,000 for the same work because
the agency didn't flinch while quoting.

The uncomfortable truth is this. Charging well is
not the opposite of being creative. It's the proof
that you take your creativity seriously.
The best creative people I know aren't the ones
who suffered for their art. They're the ones who
refused to.

I sat with this for a while. Modern self help gives
you two terrible answers - either "hustle harder"
or "renounce everything and meditate." Both felt
wrong to me.
And then I found something in Indian philosophy
that made it click. Our ancestors had already
mapped this out. Not as advice. As states of
being.

There's something called Tamas. Which means
inaction. You're not ambitious, you don't want to
do anything with your life. It sounds like peace
but it's actually not - it's numbness pretending
to be peace.
And the philosophy is very clear here: the fact
that you've been gifted a human life, you're
requested not to be in Tamas. Doing nothing is
not the answer to doing too much

Then there's Rajas. Which is hardcore ambition.
It's basically the hustle culture we talk about
today. The dark greed of wanting more and more
and more of everything, and it drives you like
mad. Here's the thing about Rajas - it feels like
progress. You're moving, achieving, ticking
boxes. But you're running on a treadmill that
speeds up every time you catch up to it.
My Koramangala friend has been in Rajas for 30
years. The bungalow is proof it works. His
restlessness is proof of what it costs.

And then there's Satvik. Which is balance. And
this is the part most people get wrong - Satvik is
not the absence of ambition. You still have the
drive for materialistic things, but only till it gives
you a good life. Not a greedy one.
You know where your "enough" is. And once you
cross it, the same drive gets redirected -
towards peace, towards meaning, towards
things money stopped buying a long time ago.

The insight that stayed with me is this - ambition
is not the villain. Unexamined ambition is. We
just keep running because everyone around us is
running.
And honestly, these are not three types of
people. They're three states you keep moving
between. Some weeks I'm in Rajas, chasing
everything. Some Sundays I'm fully in Tamas,
telling myself it's rest when it's actually
avoidance. Satvik is not a destination you reach
once. It's a direction you keep correcting
towards.
My friend in Koramangala doesn't need another
crore or another car. He needs to answer one
question - what does enough look like for him?
Have you ever actually defined yours?

It assumes that great content comes from

almost entirely underreported. Creators making

We've been typing a 4-digit PIN to pay for
groceries etc since 2016. Nobody questioned it.
It just became normal.
BHIM UPI just made it optional.

Think about what you actually do when you pay
via UPI.
You open the app. You wait. You type 4 digits
you've memorised through sheer repetition. You
hope you didn't mistype. You wait again. This
was a revolution in digital payments.
But that was 2016.

Your phone already knows it's you.
Every time you unlock it fingerprint, face, it's
running an authentication check more
sophisticated than any PIN you've ever set.
That same technology now works for UPI
payments on BHIM.
Not because it's cool. Because it was always the
more logical next step.

The way it works is straightforward.
Transactions up to 75,000 can be authorized
using your fingerprint or Face ID. The biometric
check happens on your device.
Nothing leaves your phone, nothing sits on a
server. Your PIN still works for anything above
that.
NPCI built the framework. BHIM is the first to
bring it to users.

The interesting thing about habits is that we
defend them longest when they're the most
replaceable.
PIN felt secure because it was effort. Turns out
effort and security are not the same thing.
A fingerprint is harder to replicate than a 4-digit
number someone can watch you type at a billing
counter.

Enable biometric authentication in your BHIM
app.
It takes under a minute. And then you'll wonder,
quietly, why this wasn't always how it worked.

The Diet Coke shortage is a better business
story than most MBA case studies.
Diet Coke disappeared from Blinkit, Zepto,
supermarket shelves in Bangalore, Mumbai,
Pune, and Ahmedabad over the last couple of
weeks.
And the internet did exactly what the internet
does. Memes, Reddit threads, creator videos,
"found one can" celebration posts, the works.

Here's the thing though. This isn't a supply
hiccup. This is three completely separate things
going wrong at the same time, for the same
product, right as summer starts.
The first thing is a war. Iran blocked the Strait of
Hormuz. Around 9% of global aluminium
production comes from the Gulf region. Prices
shot up 14-20% in under two months.
Coca-Cola's own distributors were apparently
told, we can't fulfil your orders, there's a
shortage because of the war.

The second thing is a regulation. In April last
year, India put aluminium cans under mandatory
BIS certification.
The rollout created a backlog, approvals slowed,
imports got stuck in compliance queues,
domestic manufacturers hit capacity ceilings.
Ball Beverage and Canpack, the two major can
makers here, were already maxed out before this
kicked in.

The third thing and this is the one that doesn't
get enough attention is that India quietly fell in
love with diet drinks.
In 2020, zero-sugar beverages were 5% of
Coca-Cola India's volumes. By 2025, 30%. Diet
Coke alone doubled year-on-year. Fitness
content, calorie tracking, the general vibe shift
around sugar happened faster than the market
expected.
And Diet Coke, unlike every other soft drink, is
sold only in cans in India. No plastic bottle
backup. When the cans ran out, it just...
disappeared

But here's what I keep thinking about. Coca-Cola
said nothing publicly. No campaign, no
explanation, no "we're working on it" post
nothing.
And people still posted celebrations when they
found a single can. The absence made it more
desirable, not less.

Most products if they disappeared from shelves
for two weeks people would just switch. Nobody
would notice. Nobody would post about it.
Diet Coke became a personality trait for a
certain kind of Indian urban consumer. And you
only find that out when it's gone.
The aluminium will sort itself out eventually. The
demand is structural, it's not going away. But the
shortage accidentally answered the most
important question in branding.
If your product disappeared tomorrow, would
your customers hunt for it, or just switch?

There was a time when Indian advertising was
genuinely world-class.
That time is over. And almost nobody is asking
why.

Watch a Fevicol ad from 1995. The confidence is
the first thing you notice. Nobody explaining the
product. Nobody listing features.
The ad just trusts you. Trusts that you're smart
enough, culturally specific enough, emotionally
present enough to get it without being told what
to feel.
The Fevicol bus. The Cadbury girl on the cricket
field. Har Ghar Kuch Kehta Hai. These weren't
trying to go viral. Viral didn't exist. They were
just trying to be true. And thirty years later,
people still remember them without being
prompted.

Now look at almost any major Indian brand
campaign from the last five years. Diverse faces
smiling. Voiceover about journeys and dreams.
Product shot. Logo. A tagline that could belong
to any brand, in any category, in any country.
You could swap the logo at the end and not
notice. That's not an accident. That's the entire
problem.

Three things killed it.
Performance marketing arrived and made
untracked spending unjustifiable. Every rupee on
brand building was a rupee that couldn't be tied
to a sale.
The people who understood what the Fevicol
bus was doing slowly lost the argument to the
people with the dashboard.

Then came the committee. Brand team,
marketing head, CMO, legal, social media
manager flagging anything that might get
ratio'd.
By the time the campaign comes out the other
side it has been so thoroughly de-risked that
only the logo survives.

And then, most painfully, Indian brands stopped
trusting Indian audiences. The old ads were
specific places, specific people, specific Hindi
with region and class baked in.
They spoke to someone, and everyone else was
overhearing. Modern Indian advertising tries to
speak to everyone at once, which means it lands
with no one in particular.

The Fevicol client once approved an ad where
the product appeared for two seconds at the
end and the entire preceding minute was an
absurd situation involving a bus, a buffalo, and
the patience of rural India.
Nobody asked about conversion rates. Someone
decided this was true and funny and worth
making, and someone else decided to trust
them.
That combination, a creative person willing to
be strange, a client willing to trust produced
some of the finest advertising any country has
ever made.
Both halves are now almost entirely gone.

What replaced them is very professional, very
safe, and completely forgettable. The brands
that figure out how to bring it back will look like
they have an unfair advantage.
They won't. They'll just be doing what used to
be normal, before the committees took over.

Last month I was having dinner with a founder
who runs a fairly large D2C jewellery brand, and
she told me something that has been stuck in
my head since.
Their best customer last year, a woman from
Coimbatore who bought close to 4 lakhs worth
of jewellery across 11 orders, has never liked a
post, never commented, and isn't even following
the brand on Instagram.

When they finally got her on a feedback call and
asked how she discovers new collections, she
said, "I screenshot the ads and send them to my
husband and my sister. We discuss on
WhatsApp. Then I order."
Basically, the entire buying journey happened in
a place the brand cannot see.

Engagement is a behaviour of people who use
social media as identity. Purchase is a behaviour
of people who use social media as a catalogue.
These are two different psychological
relationships with the same app. The 19 year old
commenting "need this" is performing taste,
because in her world, being seen wanting the
right things is social currency.
The 42 year old in Coimbatore has no audience
to perform for.
Her taste gets validated by three people on
WhatsApp, and that validation is worth more to
her than 500 likes, because those three people
will actually see her wear the jewellery.

So engagement doesn't predict purchase. In
many categories, it almost predicts the opposite.
The louder someone is about a brand publicly,
the more likely the brand is serving their identity,
not their wallet.
But here's the part that actually scares me.

Your ad platform doesn't know this. When Meta
builds a lookalike audience, it learns from the
people who engage, because that's the loudest
signal it has.
Which means every optimisation cycle, your
targeting drifts slightly more towards people
who behave like your commenters and slightly
away from people who behave like your
Combatore customer.
Your creative team sees what "performs" and
makes more of it. Your agency shows you the
engagement graph going up.

And literally nobody in this loop is lying. The
machine is honestly optimising for the wrong
human.
Which is why I've started believing that in India,
the real marketing funnel has a missing middle.
Awareness happens on Instagram.
Conversion happens on your website.
But consideration, the actual deciding, happens
in WhatsApp groups you will never enter,
between a screenshot and a family discussion,
in a language your brand team probably doesn't
write in

You can't measure that layer. You can only
design for it. Make ads that survive being
screenshotted. Put the price where the husband
can see it without clicking anything. Write
captions that make sense to the sister who has
zero context.
The founder told me they've started internally
calling this "screenshot-worthiness" and I think
that's a better creative brief than anything a
strategy deck has given me in years.
Still thinking about how many brands fired their
best creative because the people who were
never going to buy didn't engage with it :)

The power of a Social Media
A 5 Cr brand hired a VP of Social Media
for 35 LPA.
Their competitor also a 5 Cr brand hired a a social
media manager for 6 LPA.
Three years later:
Brand A: 50 Cr, crediting their VP of Social Media
Brand B: Still at 5 Cr, blaming "the algorithm"
Here's what actually happened.

What the Social Media Manager did:
→ Posted 3x a week on Instagram
→ Replied to comments
→ Ran influencer campaigns when marketing
approved budget
→ Reported: "Engagement up 15%!"
→ Sat in zero leadership meetings
What the VP of Social did:
→ Sat in product development meetings - killed 2
launches because "this won't work on social"
→ Owned customer insights - flagged complaints
that became product improvements
→ Built a content engine - 47 pieces of UGC per
month vs 12 polished posts
→ Turned social into a revenue channel - not just a
brand awareness play
→ Had P&L responsibility - 72 Cr budget, measured
in actual sales
• • •

The difference wasn't skill. It was authority.
The Social Media Manager wanted to:
• Test bold creative
• Respond to trending moments in real-time • Invest
in community building
But needed 3 approvals and a deck to do anything.
The VP of Social:
• Had the authority to move fast
• Reported to the CEO
• Could kill bad ideas before they launched
• Wasn't waiting for "brand guidelines" to react to
culture

Here's the pattern I keep seeing:
Brands treat social media like a megaphone when it's
actually your nervous system.
It's where you:
→ Hear what customers actually think (not what
surveys say
→ Test messaging before spending 750L on a
campaign
→ Build community that becomes your moat
→ Turn customers into creators
But if your "social person" has to ask permission to
reply to a viral tweet, you've already lost.

The uncomfortable truth:
Your competitor isn't beating you because they post
better. They're beating you because their social team
has a seat at the table where decisions get made.
While your social manager is waiting for approval on
a carousel post, their VP is in the room saying "we
can't launch this, it'l get destroyed on Twitter."

The shift:
STOP treating social media as a "creative" function.
START treating it as a strategic business function.
STOP hiring based on "can they make pretty posts?"
START hiring based on "do they understand
business?"
Because in 2025, your brand's reputation is built (or
destroyed) on social media faster than any campaign
you'll ever run.
And if the person managing that doesn't have the
authority to act fast, you're playing defense in a
game that rewards speed.

Travel. Get on planes, trains, buses that take you
somewhere you've never been. Get lost in cities
where you don't speak the language. Eat the
street food. Talk to strangers. Your personality
doesn't develop in your comfort zone, it
develops when you're slightly terrified and
completely alive.

Eat great food. Not just fancy food, but real
food. The stuff that makes locals line up at 5
AM. The family recipe that takes all day. The
hole-in-the-wall spot with plastic chairs and the
best dal you've ever tasted. Food is culture on a
plate. Every meal that matters teaches you
something about people, about place, about
paying attention.

Watch interesting movies. The ones that make
you uncomfortable. The ones from countries you
can't find on a map. The weird ones, the slow
ones, the ones your friends won't watch with
you. Let directors show you how they see the
world. Your perspective is just one of billions.

Read good books. Read voraciously. Read things
you disagree with. Read poetry even if you think
you hate poetry. Read history, read fiction, read
memoirs of people who lived lives nothing like
yours. Books are how you live a thousand lives in
one.

Fall in love. Stupidly, completely, recklessly. Let
someone matter to you enough that it could
wreck you.
Fall out of love. Survive it. Learn that you're
bigger than your heartbreak. Discover who you
are when you're alone again.

Make mistakes. Make glorious, embarrassing,
expensive mistakes. Fuck up. Fail publicly. Say
the wrong thing. Trust the wrong person. Start
the wrong business. Mistakes are the only real
education.

Climb mountains. Go to beaches. Jump in cold
water. Feel small next to the ocean. Feel
powerful at a summit. Get sunburned, get rained
on, get exhausted. Your body isn't a vehicle for
your head, use it, test it, feel what it can do.
Dance badly. Sing off-key. Try the thing you'll
probably suck at.
Have conversations that last until 4 AM. Fight
about ideas, not egos. Change your mind about
something important.

Your personality isn't something you're born
with and you're stuck with. It's not your zodiac
sign or your Myers-Briggs type. It's the
accumulated weight of everything you've done,
everyone you've met, everywhere you've been,
everything you've tasted and read and tried and
failed at.

The most boring people are the ones who never
leave home, never take risks, never let anything
change them. The most interesting people are
the ones with scars and stories and strong
opinions formed by experience, not inheritance.
So go. Do things. Collect experiences like their
currency because they are. They're the only
currency that makes you richer instead of poorer
when you spend it

Poker and the game of life:
Poker has always fascinated me for
it pure psychology. You get dealt a set of cards
and whether it's good or bad you have to keep
calm. One flinch and someone will notice you.
The best poker players never get attached to the
hand they're dealt.
And interestingly life, business and relationships
is similar as well.
You'll get some good cards and bad cards. And
you have the make the most of it. The reason
why Poker makes it all the more interesting is
that even if you get dealt a bad hand you can
still convert that to a winner.

You learn to make decisions with incomplete
information
In poker, you never see all the cards. You don't
know what's coming but you still have to decide.
That's the same in business, relationships or
hiring people.
You're always operating with 40% of the
information and trying to make the best call.

You stop caring about being "right"
Good poker players fold 70% of their hands.
They're comfortable saying "I don't have an
edge here" and walking away.
Most people can't do this. They've already
invested time, money, ego. So they keep going.
Poker teaches you sunk costs fallacy. The only
question is what's the right move now?"

You learn to control your emotions.
Someone just beat you with a lucky card and
you're angry. You want revenge. That's called
"tilt" in poker. And it will destroy you.
I see this in business all the time. Someone gets
rejected. Gets criticized. Gets outsmarted. Then
they make emotional decisions trying to prove
something.
Poker players know that emotions cost money.
Real money. So you learn to spot when you're
compromised and step away.

You learn to read people
In poker, everyone's lying. It's part of the game.
So you stop listening to words. You watch
actions.
Does their hand shake when they bet? Do they
go quiet or start talking? How fast do they make
decisions? You build a baseline. Then you spot
changes and this works in business too.
Poker teaches you to ignore words and watch
behavior. Not in a cynical way. You're just
separating signal from noise. Most people take
everything at face value. Then they're shocked
when the investor ghosts. When the customer
doesn't buy. When the co-founder quits.
Poker players aren't shocked. They saw it
coming. Because they watch what people do,
not what they say.

So should you learn poker?
If you want to get better at:
• Making decisions under pressure
• Reading people
• Managing your emotions
• Thinking long-term
• Letting go when you're beat
Then yes. Otherwise, don't. It's brutal. It's
humbling. It will show you every delusion you
have about yourself.
Which is exactly why it works.

Almost every other book at an airport bookstore
has "bestseller" written on the cover and it's
always made me laugh a little, because in India
there's literally no official rule about who gets to
use that word.
My book sold half a million copies, so l've spent
a lot of time around publishers and seen how
loosely it gets used.

We don't even have one list. The newspaper list
runs on something called the Nielsen data.
Amazon has its own, and then most big
bookstores keep their own lists too, so in the
same week a book can be number one in one
place and not even show up in another.
And even Nielsen, which is the closest we get to
real numbers, only tracks a part of the market.

And the number that gets you called a bestseller
here is basically 10,000 copies.
Which sounds like a typo when you think about
how many crores of people in this country read
English.
But a lot of novels don't even cross 5,000, so
when a book sells in lakhs it's genuinely rare.

Then there's the Amazon badge. That orange
"#1 Best Seller" tag works per category and
keeps updating through the day.
So if you pick a small enough category and get a
few friends to buy the book on the same
afternoon, you're a #1 bestseller for a few hours.
People have literally done this with blank
notebooks to show how easy it is.

And once you've had it, even for a few hours,
nobody's really going to take it back.
It goes on the cover of the next print run and
into the author bio, then the speaker intro and
the Linkedin headline, and it sits there for years
because nobody ever asks which list it was or
which week.

If you actually want to know whether a book
sold, flip to the page right after the title, the one
with all the tiny copyright text nobody ever
reads.
Most publishers print which reprint that copy is
from, and a book that's on its fifteenth or
twentieth reprint has basically been selling for
years, whatever list it was or wasn't on.

I don't think this makes those authors frauds or
anything, honestly the system kind of invites it.
But basically you don't need to sell a lot of
copies to become a "best-selling" author in India

The average Indian man has exactly 4 emotions
he's allowed to express.
Happy. Angry. Funny. Fine.
Everything else he was taught to bury before he
turned 10.
Swipe to read →

A boy cries at school and his father says "boys
don't cry" A teenager tells his mother he's
scared about exams and she says "just study
harder, what's there to be scared of."
A college kid tells his friends he's feeling lonely
and they say "let's go drinking ."' A 28-year-old
man going through his first real heartbreak tells
his best friend and the response is "move on
bro, plenty of fish."
Same lesson taught by different people at
different ages but always the same message
whatever it is that's happening inside, keep it
inside.

And then something happens around 28 or 30. A
relationship gets serious enough that someone
finally asks him to open up.
A girlfriend or a wife says "talk to me, tell me
what's going on, I can't read your mind." And he
genuinely doesn't know how. Not because he
doesn't want to.
Because the vocabulary was never installed. He
has feelings he has no names for. Experiences
he's never processed out loud.
Things that happened years ago that still sit
heavy but he's never once described to another
human being because there was never a
situation where that felt safe or acceptable or
even possible.

So what comes out instead is either nothing or
everything at once in the worst possible way.
The silence gets read as "he doesn't care." The
occasional explosion gets read as "he has anger
issues." The emotional shutdown during an
argument gets read as "he's cold."
But none of that is what's actually happening.
What's happening is a person trying to express
something they were never given the tools to
express, in a language they were never taught,
to someone who understandably can't tell the
difference between "I can't say it" and "I don't
feel it."

This is why men bond the way they do. Not
through conversation but through proximity.
Sitting next to each other at a bar without talking
about anything real.
Playing football every Sunday as a way of saying
"I need people around me" without actually
saying it. Sending memes at midnight as a way
of saying "I'm thinking about you" without the
vulnerability of a phone call.
The entire male friendship structure is built on
being physically present while emotionally
absent because that's the only format that
doesn't trigger the "you're being too much"
alarm that was installed in childhood.

And then we wonder why Indian men struggle in
marriages. Why they "shut down" during
conflict. Why they can't say "I'm hurt" and
instead say "I'm angry."
Why they process a job loss alone for 3 weeks
before telling their wife. Why their idea of
dealing with grief is going quiet for 6 months
and hoping it passes. It's not that they don't feel
things.
Men feel everything everyone else feels. Every
bit of fear and sadness and confusion and
tenderness. They just have nowhere to put it. No
language for it. No safe room for it.
So it sits there. Compounding. Quietly. For years.
Until it comes out sideways as rage or
withdrawal or a health problem at 45 that "came
out of nowhere" but was actually decades of
swallowed emotions showing up in the body
because they had nowhere else to go.

The few Indian men who figured out how to be
emotionally articulate didn't learn it from their
environment.
They learned it despite their environment.
Usually through a painful breakup that forced
them to look inward. Or therapy they started
secretly because even booking the appointment
felt like admitting defeat.
Or one friend usually one who broke the pattern
and said "I'm not doing great" first, which gave
everyone else permission to say it too. That's
how rare it is.
One person in a group of 12 saying something
honest can feel revolutionary. That's how low the
bar is.

What makes this worse is that nobody frames it
as a systemic problem. When Indian men can't
communicate, the conversation is always "men
need to do better" or "men need to open up" as
if the skill was available and they just chose not
to learn it.
Nobody asks who was supposed to teach them.
Their fathers didn't have it. Their grandfathers
definitely didn't have it. Their friends are in the
same boat. The school system doesn't cover it.
The culture actively punishes it.
So where exactly was this learning supposed to
come from? Telling an Indian man to "just open
up" without acknowledging that every system
around him was designed to make sure he never
does is like telling someone to swim who was
never allowed near water.

This isn't a post about blaming anyone. Not
fathers. Not mothers. Not friends. Not culture.
Everyone was doing what they knew with what
they had. But somewhere along the way an
entire generation of Indian men ended up
emotionally fluent in exactly zero languages.
They can build companies and manage teams
and solve complex problems and provide for
families and show up every single day. But ask
them what they're feeling right now right now in
this moment and most of them will pause.
Not because the answer is "nothing." But
because the answer is so much that they
genuinely don't know where to start. And
nobody ever taught them how.

These words got into group chats and Instagram
captions and dinner table conversations.
And honestly for a while it did feel like progress.
Even I spoke about it for almost 3 years.

But knowing the words doesn't mean you're
doing the thing the words are talking about.
You can know that avoidance is a trauma
response and still keep avoiding. You can know
you have attachment issues and still not have
worked through them at all.

In India therapy basically became an aesthetic
first, and the actual practice came much later, if
it came at all.
The person posting about "healing" has had like
two therapy sessions and stopped when it got
uncomfortable.
Everyone spoke about therapy but most of them
didn't actually go for therapy

Real therapy is uncomfortable, and not in a way
that makes for good content.
You sit with someone for an hour and they ask
you questions you don't want to answer, and you
walk out feeling worse than when you walked in.
You go home and think about something your
mother said in 2007 and feel an emotion that
can't be described. You cancel next week's
session because it's too much. You come back
anyway..

And honestly the worst part is what it does to
the people around them.
Someone who has all the therapy vocabulary but
hasn't really gone deep into any of it is genuinely
harder to be in a relationship with than someone
who never came across it. They can name your
behaviour patterns before you even can.
They can walk out of a conversation just by
calling it triggering. When they avoid something

thing you're being toxic.

money sure, but mostly it's that very specific
discomfort of looking at yourself properly for a
long time without looking away.
