and decided that was enough.
So now we have a generation that can diagnose
everyone around them but can't sit with their
own discomfort for more than ten minutes, and
I'm not sure that's what a mental health
revolution looks like.

How VCs Actually Decide whether to invest in
your Startup or not
Just watched a 90-minute talk between Rajan
Anandan (Peak XV), Mukul Arora (Elevation),
and Anand Daniel (Accel). These guys see
thousands of startups and have billions to
invest.
They explained exactly how they decide who
gets money and who doesn't. The honest
version you never hear in meetings.

Elevation Capital meets 5,000-10,000 startups
every year. They invest in 14. That's it. 14 out of
10,000.
Every VC does 10-15 meetings each week.
Rajan meets 5 new companies every single day.
Getting a meeting? Super easy.
Getting money? Almost impossible.

Rajan said he gives exactly 30 minutes for first
meetings. Most founders spend 15 minutes
talking about themselves and their degrees.
His response: "You haven't won the Nobel Prize
yet." Talk about yourself for 2 minutes max. Use
the other 28 minutes for one thing: tell them
something about your market that they've never
thought of before.
Mukul gave an example - Swiggy said "we'll do
our own delivery," while 50 other food
companies before them were just connecting
restaurants to customers. That one different
idea got his attention.

Rajan shared his main rule: "Would I quit my job
and work for this founder?"
Not "are they smart?" Not "is the market big?"
Would you actually leave everything and join
them?
4,000 people apply to Surge. 14 get in. He said:
"I'd work for most of them."
If you feel that strongly about someone in 15
minutes, everything else becomes less
important.

They explained what kills your chances instantly:
- Saying you have "contracted revenue" when
it's just emails or WhatsApp chats
(contracted means actual signed legal
contracts).
- Not knowing basic numbers like how many
users come back after 30 days.
- Making up answers instead of saying "I
don't know."
- Saying "I talked to hundreds of customers"
then showing 3 WhatsApp groups with 12
people total.
- Worst: when they ask to talk to your
customers and you make excuses because
those people aren't really customers yet.
They figure this out immediately. It's over.

Show Your Product Live
Both agreed: if you've built something, show it to
them live.
But Rajan warned: "Make sure it's actually good."
Don't send recorded videos - they look fake.
If something crashes during the demo, that's
fine.
But take 8 minutes and show the real product
working. Mukul made this clear - a bad demo is
worse than no demo because it kills all trust.

No" Doesn't Mean "Never"
Mukul told the Meesho story - took 18 months
from first meeting to getting investment.
Rajan mentioned Arintra - they said no first, then
invested 6 months later.
What happened? Founders kept building, didn't
change everything for VCs, and sent short
monthly emails.
Just three lines: how many customers you
added, which number went up, one good thing
that happened.
That's it. Rajan admitted: "We read everything."
Even when they don't reply, they're watching.
When your product really starts working, they
come back.

Don't Change Your Idea For VCs
Mukul was super direct: "Don't take VC
feedback too seriously. Go talk to your
customers instead."
Four VCs said no? Don't change your whole idea
to make them happy. That's a mistake.
He said the best companies in their funds made
decisions their investors disagreed with.
Customers loved those decisions, investors
didn't understand, but founders did it anyway.
What your customers think matters.
What VCs think doesn't matter as much.

They talked about Dream11. The founder Harsh
Jain met with 105 investors before one said yes.
Number 105. Kalaari finally invested. Now it's
India's biggest gaming company.
Their point: most founders give up after 10
rejections. VCs get things wrong all the time -
they're just comparing you to companies they've
seen before. Building something truly new? They
won't understand it right away.
After your first funding round, their advice: don't
go looking for more money. Just build something
great, talk about it publicly a bit, and let
investors come find you.

Their main message: VCs don't decide if your
idea is good. They decide if you can actually
build it and get customers to love it.
When they say no, it doesn't mean quit. It means
prove them wrong by getting customers.
And raising money isn't the goal. Building
something people love is the goal. Rajan said it
clearly: Getting money when customers don't
love your product yet just means you'll fail
slower.
Get 10 customers who really really love what you
built. After that, everything else becomes easier.

Why we don't have original thoughts anymore.
I recently came across a reel from a creator
where she broke down exactly why we don't
have original thoughts anymore. It was from an
article on Substack by this writer called Feifei.
And honestly, I couldn't stop thinking about it
after.
So here's what she's basically saying.

The problem isn't that you're not smart enough
to think for yourself. Your current environment
produces zero friction between you and
everything you consume.
Everything is smooth. Scroll, absorb, agree,
move on. No moment where you're required to
do anything with what just entered your brain.
There's never a moment where you're actually
forced to sit with something and go okay, what
do I think about this?

We're becoming extremely well-informed empty
vessels.
We know what Paul Graham said. We know what
the Twitter thread said. We know what the
podcast guest with the impressive background
said. We can reconstruct the argument
flawlessly.
We can even add a "I've been thinking about this
a lot" at the front of it to make it sound like ours.
But it isn't ours. And people can tell.

Feifei's fix is almost annoyingly simple. Before
you look at what anyone else thinks write down
what you actually thought. Not the smart
version.
Not the version you'd post. Just what you
actually noticed, what bothered you, what you
weren't sure about. Doesn't have to be good.
Doesn't have to be coherent.

And the part that really got me was this: the
reason we avoid forming our own opinions isn't
laziness.
It's risk management. If you share someone
else's take and it's wrong, you can distance
yourself from it. "That's just what everyone was
saying."
But if you put forward your own thought and it's
wrong? That's yours. That failure has your name
on it.

The fix isn't reading more or thinking harder. It's
just next time you finish something, close the
app, sit with the slight discomfort of not knowing
what you think yet, and stay there a little longer
than feels comfortable.
Your actual opinion is in that discomfort. Most
people just never wait long enough to find it.

Why Isn't Bollywood Making Movies for
India 1 Anymore?
The Audience That Goes to Theaters Most Is
Getting the Fewest Films

Let me break down the theater economics:
• ••
India 1 (top 50-70 million urban affluent): Goes
to 15-20+ movies per year. That's every other
weekend, sometimes more. They have
disposable income. They treat movies as regular
entertainment, not a special occasion.
India 2 (next 200-250 million aspirational middle
class): Carefully selects 5-6 movies per year.
They debate. They wait for reviews. They check
BookMyShow ratings. Movies are a calculated
expense.
India 3 (600+ million mass market): Maybe 1-2
movies annually, usually massive event films or
during festivals. Or they wait for OTT.
Now here's the insane part: Bollywood has
systematically stopped making films for India 1.
The segment with the highest theater frequency
AND the most spending power.

What Changed?
Look at Bollywood's output in the 2010s versus
now.
Then, you had:
- Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara (2011) - Road trip
across Spain, friendship, self-discovery
-English Vinglish (2012) - Urban woman,
identity, modern marriage
-Piku (2015) - Father-daughter relationship,
aging, urban quirks
-October (2018) - Unconventional love story,
emotional maturity
-Andhadhun (2018) - Dark comedy, twisty
thriller
These films spoke directly to India 1's lived
experiences. Not just their income level, their
actual psychological reality.

Now? Look at what's being made:
• •
Recent Bollywood has become obsessed with:
- Small-town stories (that India 1 has no
connection to)
- Mass-belt sensibilities (emotions pitched at
high volume)
- Pan-India appeal (code for: make it work in
Lucknow and Ludhiana)
- South cinema formulas (spectacle over story)

The Stories Being Ignored
What India 1 is starving for:
Urban generational wealth conflicts - The guilt
and complexity of inherited privilege, startup
failures, parental expectation
Modern relationship dynamics - Live-in
relationships, divorce, choosing career over
family, elder care
Cosmopolitan identity crisis - Being Indian
abroad, being "too Western" at home, code-
switching exhaustion
White collar professional life - Office politics
without caricature, startup culture, corporate
toxicity
Nuanced mental health - Depression without
redemption arcs, therapy as normal, medication
without stigma
These are 750-100 crore potential hits if made
with honesty and craft.

Why Bollywood Thinks This Won't Work
Every time someone pitches an India 1-focused
film, here's what happens:
Producer: "But this is too niche. Too limited
audience."
You don't need pan-India. You need depth of
engagement.
Producer: "These films don't get 7100 crore
openings."
You know what's better than one 7500 crore
blockbuster? Four Z120 crore hits that cost $40
crore each.
Producer: "But OTT will take this audience."
Partially true. And here's where strategy matters.

Yes, India 1 watches Netflix, Prime, Apple TV+.
Yes, they consume a lot at home.
But here's what OTT can't give them: communal
discovery of Indian stories that feel
contemporary.
When Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara released, India 1
watched it in groups. They quoted it. They
planned their own road trips. It became cultural
currency.
India 1 WANTS to go to theaters for Indian
stories that feel like they're about them. They're
just not getting those stories anymore.

What Happens If This Continues?
India 1 is already drifting away.
Not completely. They'll still show up for massive
spectacles (Jawan, Pathaan). But their regular
moviegoing habit? That's dying.
They're filling the gap with:
• International content on streaming
• Regional cinema that's more
interesting (Malayalam, Marathi)
Hollywood films
• Other forms of premium
entertainment
And once you lose the habit, you don't get it
back.

India's middle class has a dirty secret.
67% of Indian families have taken a personal
loan.
53% of Indian youth are in debt before they turn
30.
They don't look like it. That's the whole problem.
In 2016 BuzzFeed gave a name to this
phenomenon - The urban poor.

Pick any metro city. Look at the people around
you earning between 75 lakh and 730 lakh a
year the young professionals, the mid-career
managers, the startup employees with the good
job titles.
From the outside, life looks fine. The trips
happen. The cars get upgraded. The weddings
are big.
These are the urban poor.

In the last decade, personal loans as a share of
total bank credit in India went from 17% to 32%.
This is not a story about bad people making bad
choices.
It's a story about a system that made borrowing
feel normal. Digital lending apps that approve in
minutes. Credit cards with limits that arrive
before the financial literacy to use them.
A social media feed full of peers who look like
they're doing fine, which makes falling behind
feel like a personal failure rather than a
structural one.

Here's what the arithmetic actually looks like
from the inside.
By the 22nd of the month, the bank balance is
gone. Not because of one big decision but
because of dozens of small ones, each of which
felt reasonable in isolation.
What nobody shows you is the compounding.
Each loan taken to manage another loan. Each
credit card rollover that quietly grows. India's
household debt-to-income ratio was 30% in
2018. By 2022 it was 37%.

And the cost doesn't stop at money.
Debt does something to a family beyond the
balance sheet. Relationships strain. Trust
erodes. The thing that was supposed to fund a
better life starts quietly dismantling the life it
was meant to improve.
The mental health impact is real and largely
invisible because admitting you are in a debt
spiral requires admitting the image you have
been maintaining is not quite true.
And in a country where your lifestyle is your
social currency, that admission costs more than
most urban poor are willing to pay. So they keep
up the image. And the debt keeps growing
underneath it.

The economy feels it too, even if nobody
connects the dots.
When middle-class households spend their
income servicing debt instead of living their
lives, consumption slows.
India's private consumption growth was 7.9% in
2019-20. By 2022-23 it had dropped to 5.3%.
That is not a coincidence. That is millions of
urban poor families quietly pulling back because
the EMI due date arrives before the discretionary
spending can.
The virtuous cycle, earn, save, invest, grow has
been quietly replaced by a different loop.
Borrow, spend, service, repeat. It feels like
prosperity. The data says otherwise.

The cruelest part is what the urban poor look
like from the outside.
The person managing four EMIs, rolling over a
credit card, eating into whatever small savings
exist looks, on every visible axis, like someone
doing well.
The car is in the parking lot. The Instagram is
updated. The designation on Linkedin sounds
right.

The richest-looking people in your city are the
urban poor.
And the real sadness isn't that they made bad
choices. It's that nobody ever showed them an
honest picture.
Just an endless scroll of people who looked like
they were winning which turned out to be the
most expensive thing any of them ever watched.

It's called clipping and seeding
Clipping is when you take the best 15-30
seconds from longer content and turn it into a
standalone viral asset.
Seeding is when you deliberately plant these
clips across multiple platforms and communities
within a short time window to create the illusion
of organic virality.
Instead of posting the full song or trailer once
and waiting, you clip the most memeable
moment and strategically place it in hundreds of
accounts.
When people see the same clip 3-4 times across
different platforms in one day, their brain doesn't
think "this is being promoted." It thinks
"everyone's talking about this" and FOMO kicks
in. That's when real organic sharing begins.

Within hours of the film's release, short clips of
just that Akshaye Khanna entry started
appearing on Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts,
and X. Not full songs and not movie trailers.
Just that specific 15-20 second moment.
Perfectly edited with perfect aspect ratios for
each platform.
This is called seeding and the process is taking
most viral-ready moment, clipped it into
platform-optimized formats, and distributed it
through a network of accounts before the
general audience even knew what to look for.
And this happened across hundreds of
accounts.

Most of what you think is "organic virality" in
Bollywood today is actually seeded.
The difference is Dhurandhar did it with a
genuinely great moment that deserved to go
viral.
Most films seed mediocre content and wonder
why it doesn't stick.
You can't seed your way to virality with a shitty
product.
But if you've got something genuinely good,
seeding is how you make sure it doesn't get lost
in the noise.
That Akshaye Khanna scene would have
eventually gone viral anyway. But seeding
compressed what would have taken 2-3 weeks
into 48 hours.
And in the first weekend of a film's release, that
timing is everything.

Your brand account reach is dead. Instagram is
not showing your posts to your own followers.
Paid ads are hitting 8-10x CAC in most
categories. Influencer marketing ROl is in the
toilet because everyone's doing it.
Clipping and seeding is how you break through
when all traditional channels are oversaturated.
But it only works if you're clipping content that's
genuinely worth spreading, and you're seeding
these clips in communities where they actually
Dhurandhar had a 15-second unscripted dance
move that was so good, clipping it perfectly and
seeding it everywhere turned it into a cultural
moment.
What's your 15-second clip? And are you
seeding it, or just hoping it goes viral on its own?

On Developing Your Personality
• •
Travel. Get on planes, trains, buses that take you
somewhere you've never been. Get lost in cities
where you don't speak the language. Eat the
street food. Talk to strangers. Your personality
doesn't develop in your comfort zone, it
develops when you're slightly terrified and
completely alive.
Swipe to read —->

Eat great food. Not just fancy food, but real
food. The stuff that makes locals line up at 5
AM. The family recipe that takes all day. The
hole-in-the-wall spot with plastic chairs and the
best dal you've ever tasted. Food is culture on a
plate. Every meal that matters teaches you
something about people, about place, about
paying attention.

Watch interesting movies. The ones that make
you uncomfortable. The ones from countries you
can't find on a map. The weird ones, the slow
ones, the ones your friends won't watch with
you. Let directors show you how they see the
world. Your perspective is just one of billions.

Read good books. Read voraciously. Read things
you disagree with. Read poetry even if you think
you hate poetry. Read history, read fiction, read
memoirs of people who lived lives nothing like
yours. Books are how you live a thousand lives in
one.

Fall in love. Stupidly, completely, recklessly. Let
someone matter to you enough that it could
wreck you.
Fall out of love. Survive it. Learn that you're
bigger than your heartbreak. Discover who you
are when you're alone again.

Make mistakes. Make glorious, embarrassing,
expensive mistakes. Fuck up. Fail publicly. Say
the wrong thing. Trust the wrong person. Start
the wrong business. Mistakes are the only real
education.

Climb mountains. Go to beaches. Jump in cold
water. Feel small next to the ocean. Feel
powerful at a summit. Get sunburned, get rained
on, get exhausted. Your body isn't a vehicle for
your head, use it, test it, feel what it can do.
Dance badly. Sing off-key. Try the thing you'll
probably suck at.
Have conversations that last until 4 AM. Fight
about ideas, not egos. Change your mind about
something important.

Your personality isn't something you're born
with and you're stuck with. It's not your zodiac
sign or your Myers-Briggs type. It's the
accumulated weight of everything you've done,
everyone you've met, everywhere you've been,
everything you've tasted and read and tried and
failed at.

The most boring people are the ones who never
leave home, never take risks, never let anything
change them. The most interesting people are
the ones with scars and stories and strong
opinions formed by experience, not inheritance.
So go. Do things. Collect experiences like their
currency because they are. They're the only
currency that makes you richer instead of poorer
when you spend it
Build your personality. Build yourself

Every brand targeting the Indian middle class
has built their entire strategy around one
assumption.
That the middle class wants to move up. Better
apartment. Better car. Better school. Better
holiday.
The aspiration is always vertical, always upward,
always toward the next rung.
So they build campaigns around people who are
visibly richer than their target customer.
Except that's not what the Indian middle class
actually does

The Indian middle class doesn't look up. It looks
sideways. They're not buying a car because they
saw someone richer driving it.
They're buying a car because Sharma ji next
door bought one and now every morning there's
a car parked in front of his house and there's no
car in front of theirs.
They're not booking Bali because some
influencer made it look luxurious. They're
booking Bali because four couples from their
friend group went last year.
The reference point is never above them. It's
always exactly beside them.

The person who triggers the purchase isn't a
billionaire or a celebrity or even someone from a
higher income bracket.
It's the colleague two desks away. The cousin
who got married six months ago. The neighbour
whose kid just started at an international school.
The aspiration isn't "I want to become them." It's
"I cannot be the one who doesn't have that."
This is a completely different psychological
engine and almost no brand in India has
bothered to understand it.

Upward aspiration is desire. I see something
beautiful and I want it. I see a life better than
mine and I want to move toward it. It's optimistic.
The emotional register is hope.
Sideways aspiration is anxiety. It's not pulling
toward something better. It's pushing away from
being left behind. The emotional register isn't
hope. It's fear dressed up as ambition.
The Indian middle class is mostly running on the
second fuel. And fear is a far more powerful
purchase trigger than desire.

This is why this segment keeps spending money
it doesn't really have on things it doesn't really
want.
Not out of stupidity but out of a very rational
calculation about what it costs socially to be
visibly behind your peer group.
EMI culture didn't explode in India because
Indians suddenly got richer. It exploded because
it solved a sideways aspiration problem.
It let people keep pace with their peer group
without having the money to actually do it.
The purchase wasn't rational. But the social
calculus behind it was completely rational

This is why most brand campaigns targeting this
segment quietly die after launch. They sell
aspiration upward to someone buying belonging
sideways.
They show a celebrity in a penthouse when they
should be showing someone who looks exactly
like the customer's neighbour.
Someone close enough that the gap feels
closeable and the anxiety of not having it feels
real and immediate.
The brands that have actually cracked this
market aren't saying "join the elite." They're
saying "everyone around you already has this."

If you're building a brand for the Indian middle
class, the most important question isn't "what
do they want to become."
It's "who are they terrified of falling behind." Find
that person. That's your real competition. Not
the premium brand above you.
The peer sitting exactly beside your customer.
Market to the anxiety of horizontal distance, not
the dream of vertical ascent. That's the game.

India's fastest-growing "wellness" category isn't
therapy, meditation, or fitness.
It's astrology apps.
And they're not selling predictions. They're
selling certainty to a generation that has none.

You download the app at 2 AM. Enter your birth
details. Get a free reading that's vague enough
to feel true and specific enough to feel personal.
Then it tells you something is wrong. Your
Saturn is stressed. Your career house is blocked.
Your relationships have an obstacle.
The free reading ends at the problem. The
solution is behind a paywall. 7999 for a
consultation. 7499 per chat. A subscription to
keep the anxiety managed.
The product isn't the prediction. It's the anxiety
the prediction creates.

The psychology is textbook.
It's called the Barnum effect. Give someone a
statement vague enough to apply to anyone
"you often feel misunderstood by people close
to you," "you have untapped potential you
haven't fully used" and they'll rate it as highly
accurate and deeply personal. Every astrology
app opening reading is engineered around this.
But the Indian version has a second layer.
Indians don't treat astrology as entertainment.
They treat it as infrastructure. Kundli before
marriage, muhurat before business, gemstones
for luck.
These apps aren't creating belief. They're
monetising belief that already exists.

The customer isn't your grandmother. She has
her family pandit.
It's the 24-year-old in Bangalore earning 78
lakh, anxious about her relationship, her career
switch, whether she's falling behind.
She grew up in a house where these things were
taken seriously. The muscle is already trained.
The app finds her at her most uncertain and
offers the one thing no therapist or friend can
which is a definitive answer.

A good therapist tries to make you not need
them anymore. An astrology app does the
opposite.
Every reading opens a new question. Every
consultation surfaces a new concern. Every
"remedial puja" expires unless you pay again.
Retention increases with emotional distress, not
despite it.
This is a business that grows when its customers
feel worse.

These apps don't advertise as astrology. They
say "guidance,'
" "clarity," "cosmic wellness." The
Ul looks like a therapy platform. The language
borrows mental health vocabulary "healing,"
"alignment," "energy."
A therapist needs a license. An astrologer on an
app needs a login and a rating system. The user
can't tell the difference because the packaging
is identical.

Astrology isn't inherently a scam. Millions find
genuine meaning in it.
But the neighbourhood pandit knew your family,
was accountable to the community, and wasn't
sending push notifications at 11 PM saying "your
stars are shifting."
The app took a cultural practice rooted in trust
and turned it into a subscription funnel
optimised for anxiety

The most vulnerable generation in Indian history
overeducated, underemployed, career-anxious,
caught between their parents' world and a future
that won't sit still is being sold certainty at 7499
a month.
The most profitable emotion in the country isn't
greed or desire.
It's doubt. And doubt never stops needing to be
purchased again.

Most male friendships never get past surface
level. You know the ones, you can hang out,
have a good time, talk about work, movies,
whatever. But you never really know each other.
Then there are the friendships where someone
actually gets you. Where you can say what
you're really thinking. Where you don't have to
perform.
The difference? Vulnerability.

Real friendship requires knowing someone
beyond their social mask. And that only happens
when someone drops the mask first.
Think about your closest friends. When did the
friendship shift from casual to real? It was
probably a moment where one of you said
something honest.
Something you weren't "supposed" to say.
"I'm actually really struggling with this."
"I don't know what I'm doing."
"I feel completely lost right now!"
That moment. that's where the real friendship
began.

Because most of our interactions are
transactions. We're all managing impressions,
trying to seem like we have it together, avoiding
anything that might make us look weak or weird
or too much.
But friendship isn't a transaction. It's built on
actually knowing each other.
When you're vulnerable with someone, you're
saying "here's who I actually am, not just who I
want you to think I am." And that creates space
for them to do the same.
You're not connecting over shared interests or
circumstances anymore. You're connecting over
shared humanity, the messy, uncertain,
imperfect reality of being human.

It's not about dumping all your problems on
someone. It's about being honest when it
matters.
Your friend asks "how are you?" and instead of
the automatic "good, you?" you actually answer.
"Honestly? Pretty anxious about this thing. Not
sure how to handle it."
You admit you don't know something instead of
pretending you do.
You share what you're actually afraid of instead
of what you think you should be afraid of.
You talk about the thing you're insecure about
instead of only sharing the wins.

Vulnerability has to be mutual. If you're always
the one being vulnerable and the other person
never reciprocates, that's not friendship.
Real friendship is when both people feel safe
enough to be honest. To not have all the
answers. To be imperfect.
And that starts when one person takes the risk
first.

Building real friendships through vulnerability
isn't a strategy or a hack. It's just being willing to
be honest about your actual human experience
with another human.
Not performing. Not managing their impression
of you. Just being real.
The scary part? They might not reciprocate.
They might not be ready for that kind of
friendship. They might pull back.
But if they do reciprocate? If they match your
honesty with their own?
That's when you've found a real friend.

Okay so I went down a rabbit hole on how this
Roadster actually "flies" and I think I finally get
it.
There's a fan under the car that sucks the air out
from below it.
Like a vacuum cleaner stuck to the floor. It
presses the car down so hard that it can stay
stuck upside down, even when it's not moving.
Musk said it pulls up to 2G. That's how it drove
up that inverted ramp without falling off.

And I didn't realise this at first but the fan is
mostly for grip. Normal tyres give you roughly
1.26G in a corner. With the fan it can corner at
more than 2G. For a track car that's literally
huge.
Then the flying part. They're called cold gas
thrusters. You fill a tank with air at very high
pressure, open a valve, and the air shoots out of
a nozzle and pushes the car.
Same as when you blow up a balloon and let go
and it flies around the room. There's no fire or
fuel burning, it's just air.

There are two carbon fibre tanks, about 600
litres, holding around 250 kg of air, and it goes
out through 10 nozzles. The car fills the tanks
back up by itself so you don't need any special
fuel.
• ••
So when it came off the ramp upside down, the
thrusters turned it the right way up, held it in the
air for a second and put it down.
The valves are electric and can make tiny
adjustments really fast, which is basically what
stops it from spinning out of control.

The same thrusters are why it does 0-60 in
under a second. A normal car can only
accelerate as hard as the tyres can grip before
they start spinning.
The thrusters push the whole car directly, so the
tyres aren't the limit anymore. Tesla says they
make 4-5x the force the tyres can handle.
They're selling it in three versions. Performance
is the regular one with the fan and two seats.
Thrust adds thrusters at the back for
acceleration. Rocket has thrusters all around the
car and only one seat.

Also the stunts were pre-programmed. Nobody
was sitting there flying it. And it doesn't go
anywhere really, it's more of a hop.

There's a book that has sold over 5 million
copies and is quoted by every marketer on the
planet but almost nobody actually applies it
correctly and that book is Influence by Robert
Cialdini.
He spent 35 years studying why people say yes
and boiled it down to a few principles that once
you see you can't unsee, they're operating on
you every single day and you don't even know it.

I'm going to break down five of these principles
and instead of giving you textbook definitions
I'm going to show you exactly how they work
with real examples so you never look at a sale, a
negotiation, or even a conversation the same
way again.

The first principle is reciprocity. When someone
does something for you, you feel an almost
biological need to do something back.
You can't help it. It's hardwired. Here's an
example. A study was done in restaurants where
waiters brought a mint with the bill and tips went
up by 3%. When they brought two mints tips
went up by 14%.
But when the waiter brought one mint, started
walking away, then turned back and said "you
know what, for you guys let me leave an extra
one" tips went up by 23%.
Same two mints. The difference was it felt
personal and unexpected and the customer's
brain immediately went into "I need to give
something back" mode.

This is exactly why free content works better
than ads. When a brand genuinely teaches you
something useful, solves a problem for you,
gives you a template or a framework without
asking for anything, your brain starts keeping
score.
You feel like you owe them. So the next time
they launch a product you're 3x more likely to
buy not because the product is better but
because your brain is settling a debt you didn't
even know you had.
The brands that just run discount ads skip this
entirely and then wonder why nobody is loyal.

The second principle is social proof. When you
don't know what to do you look at what other
people are doing and copy them. Here's how
powerful this is.
A hotel wanted guests to reuse their towels so
they put a sign saying "help save the
environment please reuse your towel." It worked
okay. Then they changed the sign to "75% of
guests who stayed in this room reused their
towels." Reuse went up by 33%.
Nothing changed about the towels, the room, or
the environment. The only thing that changed
was people found out that other people like
them were already doing it and that was enough.

This is why reviews on Amazon matter more
than the product description. This is why
"bestseller" tags work.
This is why you check Zomato ratings before
trying a new restaurant even though you know
ratings can be gamed.
Your brain doesn't want to figure out if
something is good, it wants proof that other
people already figured it out for you.
The smartest brands don't just collect reviews
they show you reviews from people who look like
you, live like you, and had the same problem as
you because that's when social proof hits
hardest.

The third principle is scarcity. The less available
something is the more you want it.
Here's the example that blew my mind.
Researchers told one group of people to taste
cookies from a jar of ten cookies and rate them.
They told another group to taste the same
cookies but from a jar that only had two left.
Exact same cookies. The group with only two
cookies rated them significantly tastier, more
desirable, and more valuable.
Their brain literally changed the experience of
eating the cookie because there were fewer
available. This is not a marketing trick this is
your brain lying to you about reality based on
availability.

This is why "only 2 seats left" works on
MakeMyTrip, why limited drops sell out in
minutes, and why Zara produces small batches
so you feel like if you don't buy it now it'll be
gone forever.
But scarcity only works when it feels real. The
moment your audience suspects you're faking it,
the moment they see that "sale ending tonight"
timer reset the next morning, you don't just lose
the sale you lose trust permanently. Real
scarcity tied to a genuine reason is I... See more

The fourth principle is authority. We trust people
who look like they know what they're talking
about. Not because we've verified their
expertise but because our brain takes shortcuts.
This is why doctors sell you Sensodyne, why CA
friends become your default financial advisor,
and why founders who show up on camera
sharing real numbers and real failures build more
trust than any brand page ever will.

The fifth principle is commitment and
consistency. Once you say yes to something
small your brain forces you to keep saying yes to
stay consistent with who you think you are.
Here's a perfect example. Zerodha doesn't ask
you to start trading with 5 lakhs on day one.
They get you to open a free demat account.
That's it. That tiny step makes you think "I'm the
kind of person who invests" and now your brain
needs to stay consistent with that identity so
you deposit money, then you make your first
trade, then you start a SIP, then you're
comparing mutual funds at 11pm on a Tuesday.
Nobody forced you. Your brain did. That one free
account opening rewired how you see yourself.
This is why the smartest brands never ask for
the big commitment first. They ask for
something so small it feels stupid to say no and
then let your own psychology do the rest.

Marketing at its core is just mixing and matching
reciprocity, social proof, scarcity, authority and
consistency in different doses for different
situations.
-Zomato gives you free delivery credits so you
feel obligated to order again, that's reciprocity.
-Nykaa shows you "23,000 people bought this"
so you don't have to think, that's social proof.
-Boat drops a limited edition colour and your
brain panics, that's scarcity.
-A founder goes on Shark Tank and suddenly
their product feels more legit, that's authority.
-And Swiggy gets you to just install the app first
knowing that once you order once you'll order
five hundred times, that's consistency.
Read the book. It'll change how you see
everything.

I started my company when I was 22. Here are
10 things I learned that will make you hate
entrepreneurship (and that's exactly the point).
Everyone's selling you the dream. The freedom.
The impact. The "be your own boss" fantasy.
I'm here to sell you the nightmare. Because if the
nightmare doesn't excite you, you're not built for
this.

Entrepreneurship is not a career choice. It's a
mental illness you choose to have.
Normal people optimize for stability, happiness,
work-life balance.
Entrepreneurs optimize for problems. You're
literally signing up to have more stress, more
uncertainty, more anxiety than any job would
ever give you.

Your biggest competitive advantage is your
ability to be delusional.
Everyone talks about "realistic planning" and
"market validation." But here's the truth: if you
accurately assessed the odds, you'd never start.
You need to be unreasonably confident in the
face of objective evidence that you'll probably
fail.
This is not a bug. This is the feature.

The skills that make you successful are the
opposite of what society rewards.
Society rewards patience. Entrepreneurship
rewards impatience.
Society rewards playing it safe.
Entrepreneurship rewards reckless conviction.
Society rewards being agreeable.
Entrepreneurship rewards being difficult.
You're literally training yourself to be worse at
being a normal human.

You don't "overcome" rejection. You become
addicted to it.
Here's what nobody tells you: after enough
rejection, you start seeking it out. Because
rejection means you're playing big. A day
without rejection feels like you're not trying hard
enough.
You don't build resilience. You develop a twisted
relationship with pain where comfort feels like
failure.

Work-life balance is not something you failed to
achieve. It's something you actively destroyed.
And it had to die. Because balanced people
don't build companies. Obsessed people do.
The moment you accepted "balance," you
accepted mediocrity.
Your friends have hobbies. You have a company.
They think you're missing out.
You think they're playing too safe. Nobody's
wrong. You're just optimizing for different
games.

Entrepreneurship is just choosing which type of
miserable you want to be.
Job = comfortable misery. Entrepreneurship =
exciting misery.
At least pick the misery that gives you
ownership. Because here's the secret: you're
going to be stressed either way. You're going to
have anxiety either way.
Might as well have it while building something
that's yours.

Your mental breakdowns are not setbacks.
They're the curriculum.
Every panic attack about cash flow? That's the
lesson.
Every moment of crippling self-doubt? That's
the training.
Every time you wanted to quit? That's the filter
removing people who don't want it enough.
Therapy helps you cope. Entrepreneurship
requires you to stop coping and start operating
despite it.

The more successful you become, the more
isolated you get.
Success doesn't bring you closer to people. It
separates you. Your problems become unique.
Your decisions become lonely. Your perspective
becomes alien to people living normal lives.
And you can't even complain about it without
sounding like an asshole. "Oh poor you, your
company is growing." Yeah. It is.
And it's destroying me in ways I can't explain at
dinner parties.

You're not building a business. You're building a
personality disorder.
The hypervigilance. The inability to relax. The
constant scanning for threats and opportunities.
The obsessive thinking. The mood swings based
on metrics.
Congratulations. You've given yourself the
psychological profile of someone who's
traumatized.
Except you did it voluntarily. And you'll do it
again tomorrow.

The only people who truly succeed are the ones
who were already a little broken.
Show me a successful entrepreneur and I'll show
you someone who was running from something.
Or toward something they needed to prove. Or
filling a void that normal achievement couldn't
fill.
Healthy people don't do this. They really don't.
So here's my actual advice: Don't become an
entrepreneur.
Seriously.
If you can be happy doing anything else, do that
thing.
But if you read all of this and thought "this is for
me "..Welcome to the club.
We're not okay. But we're exactly where we're
supposed to be.

The paradox of expertise: the more you know,
the harder it is to communicate simply.
The smartest people I know barely post anything
on social media.
It's the curse of knowing too much.
The mediocre ones? They're building empires.
It's the curse of knowing too much.
Swipe to read -
→>

Most people assume that the more you know
about a subject, the easier it becomes to explain
The opposite is often true.
The deeper your expertise, the harder it
becomes to communicate with someone who's
just starting out.
When you spend years immersed in a field, your
brain rewires itself. Every answer branches into
ten exceptions, every principle comes with a
caveat, and every simple question suddenly
feels impossible to answer without first
explaining everything that came before it.

Experts often believe that if they leave out an
important detail, they're oversimplifying. So they
add more context, more nuance, more
frameworks and more jargon, believing they're
helping. But to the person listening, it's complex
af.
This is what psychologists call the Curse of
Knowledge. Once you've mastered something,
it's incredibly difficult to remember what it felt
like not to know it.

This is why some of the smartest people in the
world struggle to teach, sell or market their
ideas.
They explain concepts the way they understand
them today, not the way they understood them
when they first began.
They answer questions that only another expert
would ask, while the audience is still trying to
understand the basics.
It's also why expertise doesn't automatically
create influence.

Communication is a skill of empathy before it's a
skill of intelligence. Great communicators
constantly force themselves to remember what
it felt like to be a beginner.
They resist the temptation to impress people
with complexity and instead focus on removing
confusion. They don't make ideas sound
smarter. They make them feel obvious.
That's much harder than it sounds.

Anyone can make a simple idea complicated. It
takes real mastery to make a complicated idea
simple without stripping away its essence.
That's why the best teachers, founders,
marketers and leaders aren't necessarily the
ones who know the most.
They're the ones who can translate years of
experience into a single idea that someone else
can immediately understand and act upon.

The true test of expertise isn't how much you
know.
It's how little someone else has to know before
they finally understand you.

z6 in sales from one customer.

Marketing Is Just Manipulation With a Budget
Let's stop pretending.
Marketing isn't about "connecting with
customers.
It's about manipulating your psychology until
you buy something you didn't know you needed.
And the best marketers? They're just the best
manipulators.

You weren't insecure about your skin until a
skincare brand showed you 11 signs of aging.
You didn't care about your posture until an ad
told you you're silently destroying your spine.
You were fine with your phone until they
launched a new one and suddenly yours feels
outdated.
The tactic: Problem amplification
Make you hyper-aware of a flaw.
Then sell you the solution.
You weren't broken.
They just convinced you that you were.

Social proof manipulation
10,000 customers trust us!"
(8,000 were 71 trial purchases who never came
back.)
As seen on Shark Tank!
(They got rejected but hey, they were seen.)
Trusted by celebrities!
(They sent free products to 50 influencers, 1
posted about it.)
The tactic: Borrowed credibility
They can't make you trust them directly.
So they show you other people who allegedly
do.
Your brain thinks: If everyone else bought it, it
must be good.
It's not logic. It's herd mentality.

The aspirational identity con
Apple doesn't sell phones.
They sell being creative.
Harley doesn't sell bikes.
They sell being a rebel.
Lululemon doesn't sell yoga pants.
They sell being wellness-focused.
The tactic: Identity hijacking
They make the product a symbol of who you
want to be.
You don't buy the thing.
You buy the identity.
People like me use this.
Except "people like you" is a marketing
construct they created.

The reciprocity trap
Free ebook
Free webinar
Free consultation
Nothing is free.
They gave you something so you feel obligated
to give back.
And giving back means buying.
The tactic: Psychological debt
Your brain hates feeling indebted.
When someone gives you something, you feel
pressure to reciprocate.
They didn't give. They invested.
In your guilt.

The exclusivity illusion
By invitation only
Premium members only
Early access
The tactic: Status signaling
Humans want to be in the exclusive club.
So they create a velvet rope.
Even if there's nothing behind it.
You pay for the feeling of being in.

The authority costume
Dermatologist-approved
(One dermatologist they paid said it's "not
harmful.")
Clinically tested
(They tested it. Results were mediocre. But hey,
it was tested.)
Award-winning
(They entered a pay-to-play award and won.)
The tactic: Scientific-sounding bullshit
Slap on official-looking language.
Your brain registers authority.
Even if there's no substance behind it.

Manipulation isn't inherently evil.
It's psychology weaponized for profit.
The real question:
Are you okay with being manipulated?
Because you are.
Every single day.
Every ad you see.
Every product page you visit.
Every "limited time offer" you click.
Someone studied your psychology.
Identified your triggers.
And designed a message to exploit them.

What you can do:
Not avoid manipulation (impossible).
But choose who gets to manipulate you.
Ask yourself:
• Do I actually need this?
• Or do I need the feeling they're
selling?
• Am I buying the product or the
identity?
• Would I buy this if the marketing
disappeared?

This post made you feel smart for "seeing
through" marketing.
That feeling? Also manipulatable.
Brands are already designing "anti-marketing"
marketing for people like you.
Raw. Authentic. Transparent.
It's still manipulation.
Just meta.
Welcome to the game.

Alan Greenspan, the man who ran the US
Federal Reserve for 19 years, had a private
indicator he trusted more than most official data,
which was men's underwear sales.
His logic was that underwear is the one
purchase where nobody is watching you, so men
just quietly replace old with new, and sales stay
almost perfectly flat year after year.

But the moment money gets tight, it's literally
the first thing men stop buying.
Because when you're stretching a salary, you cut
the invisible stuff long before you cut anything
people can see.
So when underwear sales dipped, Greenspan
knew the middle class was quietly bleeding,
months before it showed up anywhere else.

And if you apply that lens to India right now, it
gets uncomfortable.
Jockey's volumes have been flat or falling for
quarters, the stock is down over 30% from its
high, and every earnings call has the phrase
"subdued demand" somewhere in it.

But there's a detail buried in that same data that
almost nobody talks about, which is that while
economy innerwear is shrinking, premium
innerwear is actually growing in the middle of a
slowdown.
Which basically breaks Greenspan's whole
assumption. His index worked because
underwear was just a necessity, there was no
emotion in the purchase at all.
And somewhere in the last few years, for a
certain kind of Indian man, that stopped being
true.

You can see it in brands like XYXX.
Yogesh Kabra comes from a textile family in
Surat, and the story goes that he stood in a
store in America looking at an underwear aisle
where every brand had a point of view.
He came back home, and realised Indian men
were still buying whatever three-pack their
fathers bought.

So instead of fighting for the shrinking economy
segment, he built for the guy who'd pay 3x for
better fabric on a product literally nobody else
will ever see.

And the interesting insight is this. The Indian
man who will do the destination wedding, buy
the iPhone on EMI, order the Starbucks for the
story, and all of that spending has an audience.
But somewhere along the way he also started
spending real money on the one thing nobody
will ever see him wearing. I honestly can't think
of another category where Indians spend purely
for themselves.
Maybe that's the new indicator. Not sure what
Greenspan would make of it :)

Here's a number most D2C founders don't want
to sit with. For every 10 customers who tap "Buy
Now" on your store, 3 or 4 never finish paying.
Roughly 30-40% of all D2C revenue in India
disappears at checkout. Not because the
product was wrong, because the experience
was.

Here's what most founders haven't figured out
yet. You're not losing customers at the top of the
funnel. You're losing them at the very bottom. At
the checkout.
The one moment where intent is at its peak, the
customer has basically said yes and somehow
your store talks them out of it.

Picture what a typical D2C checkout actually
looks like. You punch in your phone number, wait
for the OTP., then type out your full name, your
full address, pincode, city, state.
You then pick a payment method, try a coupon
click on the rong one, try again, and by the time
all this happens page reloads and the cart's
gone.

And then there's the real silent killer which is
COD. India's D2C world basically runs on Cash
on Delivery. But COD is also where RTO eats
your margins. Fake orders, low-intent buyers,
people who added to cart at 2 AM and woke up
with zero memory of it.
The brands pulling ahead right now aren't the
ones spending the most on acquisition. They're
the ones who cracked how to shift COD users to
prepaid without tanking the conversion rate.

This is exactly the problem GoKwik's Kwik
Checkout was built around. It's a one-tap login
across a network of 200M+ shoppers. It has
addresses auto-filled for up to 90% of users and
heckout done in under 30 seconds.
It has a Smart nudge feature that move 25%+ of
COD orders to prepaid. And A/B testing baked
into every element so you're optimising on data,
not vibes.
This isn't a upgrade to your store. It's the
difference between a funnel that leaks and one
that actually makes you money.

wrong. They treat checkout like a tech problem.
Something the dev team owns. Something that
"works fine."

your entire funnel because the customer is
already there. Already convinced. Already
holding their wallet open.
The only question left is whether your store
makes it easy enough to pay.

not saving money. You're watching it walk out
the door.
